Treatment of infections caused by resistant dematiaceous (melanized) fungi relies on effective antifungal strategies, including drug combinations that exploit different mechanisms of action. Understanding both in vitro and in vivo efficacy, as well as the pharmacologic limitations of available agents, is crucial in managing these challenging infections.

Which of the following statements accurately reflects findings regarding antifungal therapy for resistant dematiaceous fungal infections, particularly those involving Scedosporium prolificans?

1) Terbinafine is recommended for systemic infections due to its proven in vivo efficacy.   
2) Antagonism is frequently observed when combining azoles and echinocandins against Scedosporium prolificans.   
3) Triple-drug antifungal combinations provide marked survival benefits over dual combinations in animal models.   
4) Posaconazole demonstrates superior efficacy compared to amphotericin B and itraconazole in central nervous system infections.   
5) Ketoconazole consistently outperforms 5-fluorocytosine in animal studies involving dematiaceous fungi.   
6) The use of colony-stimulating factors always enhances antifungal efficacy in vivo.   
7) Synergy between voriconazole and terbinafine is only observed in studies with animal models.
answer: The correct answer is 4) Posaconazole demonstrates superior efficacy compared to amphotericin B and itraconazole in central nervous system infections..

Microcystis species are cyanobacteria responsible for harmful algal blooms in freshwater systems, and their survival strategies in response to environmental changes are of increasing scientific and ecological concern. Genetic mechanisms, including genome rearrangement and gene regulation, play crucial roles in their adaptation during bloom cycles.

During the late stages of a Microcystis bloom, which genomic process is most strongly implicated in enhancing the population's adaptation to environmental stressors, particularly as nutrient sources fluctuate?

1) Lateral gene transfer mediated by bacteriophages   
2) Up-regulation of transposase genes leading to increased activity of insertion sequences   
3) Structural amplification of toxin synthesis operons   
4) Horizontal acquisition of photosynthesis-related plasmids   
5) Elevated expression of ribosomal protein genes   
6) Constitutive activation of heat shock protein genes   
7) Suppression of nitrate uptake transporters
answer: The correct answer is 2) Up-regulation of transposase genes leading to increased activity of insertion sequences.
text: study ( Figure S7b ), suggesting depressed growth of Microcystis spp. in the late bloom season responding to the dynamics of environmental factors, including nutrients. Along with growth, the evolution and adaptation of populations of Microcystis may be critical in its survival after bloom peak occurs. Transposases are thought to be the most ubiquitous genes in nature and play bene ﬁcial roles in environmental adaptation by means of o ﬀering selective advantage to the host genomes. 71,72Transposase genes encode DNA-binding enzymes that catalyze “cut/copy-and-paste ” reactions promoting the movement of DNA segments (i.e., insertion sequences, ISs) to new sites.73Previous studies have found extremely high content of mobile ISs (>10% of thegenome) in M. aeruginosa NIES 84374,75and have linked their expression to the nutrient sources the cells were consuming.38,54 InMicrocystis , these transposases are thought to provide a higher degree of genomic plasticity and potentially stronger adaptationcompared with other cyanobacteria in freshwater ecosystems.During this study, we observed 202 genes encoding trans-posases that were di ﬀerentially expressed in the late bloom season, of which 189 of them were up-regulated with a majorityof them belonging to the IS605 family ( Table S5 ). This suggests active genomic rearrangement to adapt to the changedenvironment of the late bloom months. These observationsprovide support for the idea that nutrient sources not only drivebiomass accumulation but also may alter the genomicarchitecture (and thus evolutionary trajectory) of Microcystis populations. Our observations point to key changes in microbial physiology (via cellular transcriptomes) that occur throughoutthe bloom season as cells shift from active bloom formation topopulation maintenance. These same observations and theinformation provided in this study also highlight thecomplicated nature of bloom dynamics with respect toMicrocystis populations and toxin production: it is becoming increasingly clear that no single variable promotes or constrainsthese populations. Moving forward, understanding why andhow blooms occur will require data collected not only at thelevel of individual species but also at the level of environmental populations and likely in consideration of the entire microbial community within individual systems. ■ASSOCIATED CONTENT *SSupporting Information The Supporting Information is available free of charge on theACS Publications website at DOI: 10.1021/acs.est.8b01066 . Bacteria living in terrestrial environments often face desiccation stress, which can threaten their survival and limit their ecological or agricultural functions. Understanding the molecular mechanisms that enable some bacteria, such as Bradyrhizobium japonicum, to tolerate dehydration is important for both basic biology and applied sciences.

Which molecular response is specifically and consistently associated with desiccation tolerance in Bradyrhizobium japonicum and many other bacteria?

1) Upregulation of nitrogenase enzyme genes   
2) Repression of ribosomal protein synthesis   
3) Induction of trehalose synthesis genes   
4) Increased production of photosynthetic pigments   
5) Activation of flagellar motility genes   
6) Enhanced expression of cell wall hydrolases   
7) Suppression of quorum sensing pathways
answer: The correct answer is 3) Induction of trehalose synthesis genes.

Genome-wide transcrip- tional analyses of desiccated versus fully hydrated cells in-dicate that several classes of B. japonicum genes are induced in response to desiccation stress. 2) The Bradford Hill criteria

question:
Facultative anaerobic bacteria employ various regulatory proteins and metabolic pathways to adapt to changes in oxygen availability. Escherichia coli and Shewanella oneidensis are model organisms for studying differences in respiratory regulation and metabolic flexibility among bacteria.

Which of the following statements accurately distinguishes the regulatory systems involved in oxygen sensing and metabolic control between Escherichia coli and Shewanella oneidensis MR-1?

1) In E. coli, Crp is the primary regulator of anaerobic respiration, while EtrA fulfills this role in S. oneidensis.   
2) Fnr directly senses oxygen in E. coli, but its analog EtrA in S. oneidensis does not significantly regulate gene expression in response to oxygen.   
3) Both E. coli and S. oneidensis utilize ArcB as the sole sensor kinase in their Arc two-component systems.   
4) S. oneidensis primarily regulates TCA cycle genes via its Arc system, similar to E. coli.   
5) In both E. coli and S. oneidensis, the Arc system controls anaerobic respiration genes in the same manner.   
6) Crp is dispensable for anaerobic respiration in S. oneidensis because EtrA compensates its function.   
7) E. coli cannot ferment, whereas S. oneidensis readily ferments despite lacking fermentation genes.
answer: The correct answer is 2) Fnr directly senses oxygen in E. coli, but its analog EtrA in S. oneidensis does not significantly regulate gene expression in response to oxygen..

Anderson Cancer Center, Houston, Texas, United States of America Introduction Depending on the availability of electron donors and acceptors, facultative anaerobes such as Escherichia coli adopt three different metabolic modes: aerobic respiration, anaerobic respiration, and fermentation [1–2]. Aerobic respiration with oxygen as the terminal electron acceptor (EA) is the most productive mode due to complete oxidation of a growth substrate while anaerobic respiration can only oxidize a substrate partially with alternative electron acceptors, such as nitrate. Fermentation is the least productive process because only substrate level phosphorylation occurs. As a result, aerobic respiration is preferred over anaerobic respiration, which in turn is preferred over fermentation [3]. Since molecular oxygen confers enormous energetic benefits, it is not surprising that changes in its availability lead to substantial changes in E. coli physiology. Several sensing systems are employed inE. coli to monitor environmental oxygen and cellular redox state. The switch between aerobic and anaerobic metabolism iscontrolled primarily by the Fnr ( fumarate nitrate regulator) transcription factor and the Arc ( aerobic respiration control) two-component regulatory system [3]. Fnr, synthesized under both aerobic and anaerobic conditions, is able to sense oxygen directly using its [4Fe-4S]2+cluster whereas the Arc system senses oxygen indirectly [4]. After sensing changes in the redox state of the quinone pool elicited by oxygen limitation, ArcB, the sensor kinase of the system, autophosphorylates and then transphosphorylates the response regulator ArcA [5–6]. Shewanella oneidensis MR-1 is a facultative Gram-negative anaerobe with remarkable anaerobic respiration abilities that allow the use of a diverse array of terminal EAs [7]. Although little is known about how this bacterium adopts different metabolicmodes in response to the availability of oxygen, surprising observations have been made. First, S. oneidensis does not ferment, although genes encoding many enzymes of mixed acid fermenta- tion are present in the genome [8]. Second, EtrA ( electron transport regulator A), the analog of E. coli Fnr, appears to have no PLoS ONE | www.plosone.org 1 December 2010 | Volume 5 | Issue 12 | e15295 significant role in mediating gene expression in response to oxygen availability [9–10]. Third, it is evident that Crp ( cyclic-AMP receptor protein) is crucial in anaerobic respiration because crp mutants are defective in utilizing several EAs, including Fe3+, Mn4+, nitrate, fumarate, and dimethyl sulfoxide (DMSO) [11]. Fourth, S. oneidensis possesses an atypical Arc system in which function of ArcB is fulfilled by two proteins ArcS and HptA [12]. Unlike the Arc system in E. coli , this atypical system appears to be important in aerobic respiration and is not involved in regulationof TCA genes [13]. In the present study, we report results from experiments designed to reveal the involvement of three global regulators(ArcA, Crp, and EtrA) in aerobic and anaerobic respiration

Transcriptional regulation in bacteria involves complex networks where global regulators can have species-specific roles. In Shewanella oneidensis, the interplay among ArcA, Crp, and EtrA differs significantly from the regulatory relationships observed in Escherichia coli.

Which statement best describes the regulatory relationship between EtrA and arcA in Shewanella oneidensis, and what is its physiological implication?

1) EtrA directly activates arcA expression, leading to increased ArcA protein levels under anaerobic conditions.   
2) EtrA represses arcA expression indirectly, but loss of EtrA does not produce a notable phenotype, indicating ArcA function depends more on its phosphorylation state than its abundance.   
3) EtrA and ArcA both directly activate each other's expression, resulting in positive feedback under aerobic conditions.   
4) EtrA does not regulate arcA expression, and ArcA levels are solely controlled by Crp.   
5) EtrA and Crp directly repress arcA, and their absence causes severe growth defects in all environments.   
6) EtrA indirectly activates arcA, but ArcA abundance is irrelevant due to post-translational modifications.   
7) EtrA directly represses arcA, with the repression causing ArcA to be completely absent in etrA mutants.
answer: The correct answer is 2) EtrA represses arcA expression indirectly, but loss of EtrA does not produce a notable phenotype, indicating ArcA function depends more on its phosphorylation state than its abundance..

question:
Bacteria deploy multiple DNA repair pathways to survive damaging ultraviolet (UV) radiation, including both photoreactivation and nucleotide excision repair. Genetic manipulation allows researchers to dissect the contributions of individual DNA repair genes to cellular resistance against UV-induced damage.

Which of the following best explains why a Pseudomonas aeruginosa strain lacking both photolyase (phr) and uvrA genes would exhibit greater UV-B sensitivity than strains lacking only one of these genes?

1) Loss of both light-dependent and excision repair mechanisms eliminates major pathways for repairing UV-induced DNA damage.   
2) Double mutant cells produce excess reactive oxygen species that increase UV-B damage independently of DNA repair.   
3) The presence of both gene deletions accelerates cell division, making cells more vulnerable to UV-B.   
4) Both genes encode the same enzyme, so deleting both has a redundant effect.   
5) Absence of photolyase alone causes maximum UV-B sensitivity, so uvrA deletion has no further impact.   
6) Disruption of both genes leads to increased expression of efflux pumps, reducing UV resistance.   
7) Double mutants import more UV-B-absorbing compounds, increasing susceptibility.
answer: The correct answer is 1) Loss of both light-dependent and excision repair mechanisms eliminates major pathways for repairing UV-induced DNA damage..

In clinical mycology, accurate identification of black molds is crucial for guiding patient management and public health interventions. Laboratory identification integrates phenotypic features, physiological tests, and optimal culture conditions to distinguish among diverse species and genera.

Which combination of diagnostic features and laboratory practices most reliably enables species-level identification of a neurotropic black mold such as Cladophialophora bantiana?

1) Exclusive use of macroscopic colony color observation on nutrient agar   
2) Reliance on molecular sequencing without phenotypic evaluation   
3) Combined assessment of macroscopic and microscopic morphology, supplemented by physiological tests on plant-based media like potato dextrose agar   
4) Observation of pigment production on blood agar only   
5) Identification based solely on growth rate at room temperature   
6) Use of cycloheximide tolerance testing as the sole criterion   
7) Limiting analysis to genus-level identification using saline wet mount preparations
answer: The correct answer is 3) Combined assessment of macroscopic and microscopic morphology, supplemented by physiological tests on plant-based media like potato dextrose agar.
text: several factors, suchas the genus of the organism recovered, whether or not anepidemiologic investigation is warranted, and/or the level ofidentiﬁcation required for appropriate patient management.The phenotypic identiﬁcation of black molds is based primarilyupon their macroscopic morphology (color, growth rate, andgrowth characteristics on standardized media), their micro-scopic morphology (hyphae, conidiogenous cells [specializedcells that produce the conidia], conidia [asexual reproductivepropagules], etc.), and a limited number of physiologic features(primarily cycloheximide tolerance, nitrate assimilation, ureahydrolysis, and growth at various salt concentrations). Onlygenus-level identiﬁcation may be possible or required for gen-era with several similar, closely related species, such as de-scribed above for Exophiala. In some other genera, certain species are clearly associated with a particular type of mycosis,and a combination of morphologic features, temperature, andphysiology can provide a species-level identiﬁcation. This is thecase for the agent of cerebral phaeohyphomycosis, Cladophia- lophora bantiana. Macroscopic morphology. The medium (see “Isolation Pro- cedures and Culture” in Diagnosis below) is an importantconsideration in the identiﬁcation of melanized fungi. The useof a medium that promotes growth most consistently matchingthe original description of the organism is preferred, and thistypically is a plant-based medium. The most commonly used ispotato dextrose agar (PDA) or variations thereof. It providescolony colors that are close to those originally described, and itis usually adequate for conidiation. Other plant-based mediainclude malt extract agar, V-8 juice agar, cereal agar, carnationleaf agar, cornmeal dextrose agar, and others. A more com-plete list of media and reagents may be found in the Manual of Clinical Microbiology , 9th ed. (441), and in the Atlas of Clinical Fungi , 2nd ed. (175). Phaeoid molds vary considerably in their colony colors. Although this characteristic is highly dependentupon environmental conditions, it is one that can be useful inthe initial separation of genera/species. While most species arevarious shades of pale gray to dark gray to black, others may bebrown or very pale or may turn darker only with the productionof certain structures. Others may be some shade of purple ordistinguished by diffusible pigments. Microscopic morphology and pleomorphism. Variable mi- croscopic morphology in the same fungus, also referred to aspleomorphism or pleoanamorphism, is another feature usefulin the phenotypic identiﬁcation of black molds. Their mode of action and structural properties are crucial factors in their therapeutic potential.

Which of the following best explains how antimicrobial peptides (AMPs) achieve selective toxicity against microbial cells while sparing host cells?

1) AMPs inhibit host cell protein synthesis more effectively than in pathogens.   
2) AMPs preferentially bind to anionic lipid-rich membranes commonly found in bacteria.   
3) AMPs require specific microbial enzymes for activation within the host.   
4) AMPs are only produced in response to viral infections in host tissues.   
5) AMPs target bacterial DNA replication machinery directly.   
6) AMPs depend on the presence of peptidoglycan to exert their effects.   
7) AMPs accumulate in the host cell nucleus to enhance immune signaling.
answer: The correct answer is 2) AMPs preferentially bind to anionic lipid-rich membranes commonly found in bacteria..
text: Title: Antimicrobial Peptides and their Pore/Ion Channel Properties in Neutralization of Pathogenic Microbes. Year: 2015 Paper ID: bf931054e3d5802afd5bb9e30ab17dcae771d6cf Abstract: The essence of successful antimicrobial chemotherapy lies in selective toxicity of the agent towards the pathogen. An ideal antimicrobial agent should kill pathogens effectively with little or no effect on host cells. There is a dearth of antibiotic and antimicrobial therapies due the rapid development of microbial resistance to these agents, as evidenced by increasing incidences of hospital acquired infections. This challenge necessitates the discovery and development of novel and effective antimicrobial agents. One promising approach is Antimicrobial Peptides (AMPs), which are synthesized by a large number of organisms. The presence of AMPs throughout evolution hints at their importance. The first and foremost interaction between AMPs and target cell occurs at the membrane of the pathogen. The details about these interactions will pave way for the development of new synthetic analogues or modified analogues of existing AMPs. Mechanistic insights into adoption of different structures in presence of bacterial membranes (and with their specific targets) will enhance our understanding and knowledge about these agents and their detailed mechanism of action. AMPs interact with lipids and form lipid-AMP complexes that create AMP-lined ion channels, which in turn modulate the membrane potential. This may have an effect on various biological processes leading to arrest of cell growth or cell death. This review summarizes the ion channel formation property of AMPs as an effective approach in dealing with neutralization of pathogenic microbes.

Nanoparticles are increasingly used in oral drug delivery, but their performance in the gastrointestinal (GI) tract depends on a range of physicochemical and biological factors. Understanding how these factors influence nanoparticle stability, dissolution, and interactions with the gut microbiota is crucial for the development of safe and effective nanomedicines.

Which factor is most likely to cause rapid dissolution and premature release of active compounds from acid-soluble nanoparticles such as ZnO during their transit through the GI tract?

1) Neutral pH in the small intestine   
2) Presence of pancreatic enzymes   
3) High surface area-to-volume ratio of nanoparticles   
4) Stable polymeric coatings resistant to enzymatic degradation   
5) Low pH in the stomach   
6) Interactions with gut microbiota   
7) Reduced fluid composition variability
answer: The correct answer is 5) Low pH in the stomach.
text: the pH and composition of the ﬂuid in the gastrointestinal tract, but also on the duration of exposure. Major pH changes along the oro-gastrointestinal tract signiﬁcantly inﬂuence the dissolution and subsequent mechanisms of ingested nanoparticles. At low pH the dissolution of nanoparticles is increased and enzymes in the digestive ﬂuids can induce rapid denudation of particles. The inﬂuence of dissolution seem to vary among nanoparticles, according with their size, being more pronounced for smaller particles as they agglomerated to a higher degree [ 72]. Additionally, particle coating may play a key role in the dissolution and also in the release of active compounds. Acidic pH induces a faster dissolution of highly acidic soluble nanoparticles, such as ZnO, while nanostructures with lower solubility in acid solutions, such as SiO 2, agglomerate in the gastric ﬂuid and are more difﬁcult to be subjected to dissolution [ 73]. Variation in the pH within the gastrointestinal compartments also alter the surface chemistry of nanoparticles, particularly in those where zeta potential is highly dependent on pH (e.g., chitosan) [74]. Understanding parameters of dissolution in gastrointestinal ﬂuids may help predict uptake and blood concentrations of the bioactive compounds contained in the nanostructured drug delivery system. However, being a very complex and diverse environment, the mechanism of action of functional nanoparticles in the gastrointestinal tract is difﬁcult to accurately predict and their physiological and chemical behavior in the gut is especially believed to play a very important role in the outcome of the disease treatment. 5. Conclusions and Perspectives The exponential growth in microbiome research and the necessity to develop novel antimicrobial drugs that will prevent dysbiosis and, hence, disease has led to a number of novel entrepreneurial avenues with great potential. This review highlighted the current developments in nanotechnology in biomedicine and its relations to microbiota. Nanostructured materials bring a new perspective to numerous ﬁelds from industry to medicine, but their impact on human health is far from being understood. It is clear that extensive research has to be conducted in order to elucidate the relevant mechanisms and impacts of nanoparticles within the gastrointestinal route, on the gastrointestinal tract components, and especially their interaction with microbiota. Interestingly, recent studies bring fascinating new evidence revealing the possibility of clear and bi-oriented interactions between nanoparticles and members of the human microbiota. One clear conclusion is that any nanostructure that reaches or transit the gastrointestinal tract has the potential to interfere with microbiota and lead to dysbiosis, thus impacting on the health of the host and also on the outcome of the applied nanotherapy. This observation needs coordinated and highly focused attention since the scientiﬁc clariﬁcation of these pathways may provide new avenues for the discovery of novel treatments for disease which require gastrointestinal therapy. Antisense Oligonucleotides (ASOs) The antisense oligonucleotides (ASOs) are short fragments of a nucleic acid that can block a pre-deﬁned target due to its complementarity. They were ﬁrst described in 1978 by Zamecnik and Stephenson, who reported a blockage in viral replication and protein translation of a sarcoma virus RNA, after exposure to an antisense 13-nucleotide-long oligodeoxynucleotide in vitro [43]. Since this ﬁrst generation of ASOs, several modiﬁcations have been made to overcome important limitations and enable clinical application such as incorporating 20-O-methyl (20-OMe) in the DNA backbone [ 44], connecting the DNA ribose ring by a methylene bridge between 20-O and 40-C atoms- locked nucleic acid (LNA) technology [45], or even using peptide nucleic acids (PNA) [46]. Antisense oligonucleotides can be used to interfere with essential biological processes of bacteria, which is helpful against bacterial infections. They can target many mRNA encoding essential genes, as well as functional domains of both 23S and 16S rRNA. Apart from targeting the essential mRNA and rRNA, ASOs can target non-essential genes related to bioﬁlm formation, as many bacterial species form extracellular bioﬁlms, making infec- tions extremely challenging to eradicate. Some examples of bioﬁlm-related genes are motA gene, encoding the element of the ﬂagellar motor complex, the efaA gene, which plays an important role in the adhesion of bacteria to surfaces [ 46,47]. ASOs can also block two- component signal transduction systems, such as VicRK, that induce the gene expression for the synthesis of extracellular insoluble glucan, an extracellular matrix component of bioﬁlms [48]. Biomaterial-based therapy has huge potential as biomaterial carriers can sustain slow- releasing drugs. Future development of new coating materials that can prevent the adhesion and subsequent bioﬁlm formation of bacteria on dental implants, based on therapeutic antisense oligonucleotides, could be the key to ﬁghting periodontitis. The use of essential oils as natural additives in food preservation has gained traction due to their antimicrobial and antioxidant properties. Food technologists and microbiologists are particularly interested in the molecular mechanisms and efficacy of essential oils against different types of foodborne microorganisms.

Which of the following best explains why Gram-negative bacteria are generally more resistant to essential oils compared to Gram-positive bacteria?

1) Gram-negative bacteria possess an outer membrane rich in lipopolysaccharides that acts as a barrier to hydrophobic compounds.   
2) Gram-negative bacteria have a thicker peptidoglycan layer, preventing entry of essential oils.   
3) Gram-negative bacteria rapidly metabolize terpenoids into non-toxic substances.   
4) Gram-negative bacteria produce higher levels of endogenous antioxidants that neutralize essential oils.   
5) Gram-negative bacteria lack cell wall structures, making them less permeable to essential oils.   
6) Gram-negative bacteria secrete polysaccharide capsules that absorb essential oils before they reach the cell membrane.   
7) Gram-negative bacteria express efflux pumps exclusively for phenylpropanoids, expelling essential oils from the cell.
answer: The correct answer is 1) Gram-negative bacteria possess an outer membrane rich in lipopolysaccharides that acts as a barrier to hydrophobic compounds..

Therefore, there is a need for alternative natural compounds that can perform the same function of common additives or can be used as an alternative to antibiotics. One such possibility is the use of essential oils (EOs) due to their known antimicrobial, antioxidant, immunomodulatory, and food preservative activities [ 7]. In line with this, several studies have described the antibacterial activity of EOs, underlying their e ective use on multidrug-resistant strains [8,9]. EOs, also known as “volatile oils”, are complex mixtures of volatile compounds that are produced by aromatic plants as secondary metabolites. They are responsible for the aromatic plant’s properties, and for this reason, they are characterized by their strong smells [ 10]. In general, EOs are liquid, volatile, and soluble in lipids and organic solvents. They can be present in all plant organs, including buds, ﬂowers, leaves, seeds, stems, ﬂowers, fruits, roots, wood, or bark. Di erent extraction techniques are widely employed for the extraction of EOs such as steam distillation, solvent extraction, and supercritical ﬂuid extraction [ 11,12]. These EOs are characterized by the presence of variable mixtures of bioactive compounds, mainly terpenoids, especially monoterpenes and sesquiterpenes. Some of them also contain nonterpenic compounds biogenerated by the phenylpropanoid pathway, such as eugenol, cinnamaldehyde, and safrole [ 13]. These bioactive compounds are responsible for the biological properties of EOs. Among them, terpenoids are the bioactive compounds that have a more important role in pathogen resistance [ 14]. Speciﬁcally, monoterpenoids a ect the multiplication and development of microorganisms by interfering with their physiological and biochemical processes during their development and multiplication [ 15]. Cinnamon bark oil is one of the most e ective EOs against common foodborne pathogens [ 16]. It should be noted that the e ect of EOs on bacterial growth will depend on whether they are Gram-positive or Gram-negative bacteria, since the lipopolysaccharide (LPS) layer in Gram-negative bacteria acts as a barrier for macromolecules and hydrophobic compounds such as those present in EOs [ 15]. Using EOs to extend the shelf life of ﬁsh and meat has also been reported in previous studies. Examples include the preservative e ect of lemon EOs on salted sardines [ 17], the e ect of chitosan coatings enriched with cinnamon oil on the quality of rainbow trout (Oncorhynchus mykiss ) during refrigerated storage [ 18], and the lengthening of the storage period of red sea bass by means of clove, cumin, and peppermint oils or poultry meat in thyme oil [19]. The antioxidant activity of EOs is another biological property of great interest because they may preserve foods from the toxic e ects of oxidants [ 20]. question:
In bacteria, the response to oxidative stress is tightly regulated by transcriptional regulators that often control the expression of genes involved in detoxification and DNA repair. The organization of certain genes in operons can provide coordinated responses to environmental challenges such as the presence of reactive oxygen species.

Which of the following statements best explains the functional significance of the overlapping stop codon of oxyR and start codon of recG in Pseudomonas aeruginosa?

1) It ensures that recG is only transcribed when oxyR is inactivated by oxidative stress.   
2) It allows for independent transcription of recG under non-stress conditions.   
3) It suggests that recG is translated using a different ribosome binding site from oxyR.   
4) It indicates that oxyR and recG are part of the same operon, leading to their coexpression from a single promoter.   
5) It prevents oxyR and recG from being regulated by the same transcriptional activators.   
6) It causes recG to be post-transcriptionally regulated by oxyR protein levels.   
7) It results in the formation of separate mRNA transcripts for oxyR and recG.
answer: The correct answer is 4) It indicates that oxyR and recG are part of the same operon, leading to their coexpression from a single promoter..

Laboratory and field studies have revealed complex cell cycle behaviors that impact their ecological role in oceanic primary production.

Which scenario most directly explains the occurrence of a second wave of cell division in Prochlorococcus populations under laboratory conditions?

1) Increased availability of nitrogen leading to more uniform cell division timing   
2) Reduced grazing pressure during daylight hours   
3) Synchronization of cell cycles to a constant temperature environment   
4) Attainment of high light intensity sufficient to enable rapid cell cycles   
5) Introduction of mixed microbial populations causing competition   
6) Extended duration of the dark period beyond 24 hours   
7) Decreased salinity levels causing osmotic stress
answer: The correct answer is 4) Attainment of high light intensity sufficient to enable rapid cell cycles.

question:
In aquaculture, probiotics are increasingly used to enhance health and disease resistance in cultured species. Evaluating their effectiveness requires careful experimental design and consideration of various biological and regulatory factors.

Which of the following is a critical step to ensure that a candidate probiotic not only demonstrates efficacy in laboratory conditions but is also viable and responsible for use in commercial aquaculture operations?

1) Relying exclusively on in vitro experiments to assess pathogen inhibition   
2) Monitoring growth rates only during the first week after probiotic introduction   
3) Conducting long-term in vivo challenge tests with regular quantification of pathogen levels and host mortality   
4) Selecting probiotics based purely on their ability to outcompete existing microbiota in isolation   
5) Applying probiotics only via water immersion, regardless of the cultured species   
6) Skipping pilot studies to accelerate regulatory approval   
7) Assuming that all probiotics are safe for native ecosystems without further testing
answer: The correct answer is 3) Conducting long-term in vivo challenge tests with regular quantification of pathogen levels and host mortality.
text: Evaluation of Potential Probiotic Effects on the Host The effect of candidate probiotics should be tested in vivo as well. When the probiotic effect is supposed to be nutritional,the candidate probiotics could be added to the culture of theaquatic species and their effect on growth and/or survival pa-rameters could be assessed. However, when biological controlof the microbiota is desired, representative in vivo challengetests seem to be the appropriate tool to evaluate the potentialeffect of the candidate probiotic on the host. Mode of application of the putative probiotic. The putative probiotic can be added to the host or its ambient environmentin several ways: (i) addition to the artiﬁcial diet, (ii) addition to VOL. 64, 2000 PROBIOTICS AS CONTROL AGENTS IN AQUACULTURE 667 the culture water (140), (iii) bathing (5, 117), and (iv) addition via live food (23, 46, 107). Experimental infections—in vivo antagonism tests. The next important step in the in vivo challenge test involves ex-perimental infection with a representative pathogen. Patho-gens or opportunistic pathogens can be administered via thediet (live food or artiﬁcial), through immersion, or via theculture water, similarly to the probiotics. In experiments per-formed by Gildberg et al. (43), Atlantic salmon fry was chal-lenged with cohabitant ﬁshes which were previously infectedwith Aeromonas salmonicida through intraperitoneal injection. The mortality of the challenged ﬁshes due to acute furunculo-sis was monitored over time. In vivo challenge tests to detect probiotic effects should be performed with great caution. The long-term effects should bestudied to determine how the pathogen is evolving. It is im-portant to observe whether the growth or the activity of thepathogen in the location where the antagonism of the probioticis expected is really suppressed or if it is only delayed, maybesimply due to some competition for nutrients. This can beillustrated by the work of Gildberg and Mikkelsen (44). Attwelve days after infection of Atlantic cod fry with a pathogenicV. anguillarum strain, reduced cumulative mortality was ob- served in ﬁsh given feed supplemented with Chaetoceros diver- gens. At 4 weeks after the infection, however, the same cumu- lative mortality as in the control treatment was reached. Theauthors argued that “this does not exclude the possibilitythough, that such methods may be of considerable importanceunder normal rearing conditions in the presence of moderatelevels of opportunistic bacteria.” In contrast, Gibson et al. (42)observed a clear decrease in the level of the pathogen V. tubiashii in a culture of oysters when Aeromonas media was added, although the probiotic strain itself could no longer bedetected in the culture after 4 days. This shows the necessity torecord mortality or disease over a long period after experimen-tal infection. Moreover, the pathogen should be quantiﬁedregularly in the culture. The gut microbiome of animals such as chickens, humans, and pigs performs essential metabolic and physiological functions, with some variation reflecting host diet, lifestyle, and intestinal physiology. Differences in microbiota composition and function can influence nutrient absorption, resistance to pathogens, and overall health.

Which of the following is most strongly associated with the increased abundance of Actinobacteria and higher microbial diversity observed in the gut microbiota of free-range chickens compared to battery-cage chickens?

1) Greater exposure to a wide variety of environmental microbes   
2) Increased intake of processed feed supplements   
3) Enhanced enzymatic digestion in the foregut   
4) Reduced availability of nutrient substrates in the intestine   
5) Prolonged digestive transit time in the hindgut   
6) Frequent antibiotic use in outdoor settings   
7) Decreased microbial fermentation in the cecum
answer: The correct answer is 1) Greater exposure to a wide variety of environmental microbes.

The observed differences were associated with lifestyles, as free-range chickens were exposed to the outdoor environment and came into contact with more diverse microbes that shape their different gut microbiota. Distinctive characteristics of chicken foregut and hindgut metagenomes Distinguished by the difference in morphology and func- tion, the chicken intestinal tract can be divided into the foregut and hindgut. Substantial microbial fermentation occurs in the cecum, which provides nutrients, detoxifies some harm- ful substances, and also helps to prevent pathogen colonization [ 20,21]. Which combination of properties most directly contributes to improved visible-light photocatalytic activity and high-temperature stability in TiO₂ materials?

Methods such as parsimonious flux balance analysis (pFBA) and flux sampling are used to characterize how metabolic pathways adapt at different growth rates.

When analyzing central carbon metabolism in glucose-limited Komagataella phaffii, which scenario most accurately describes the correlation between flux through glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase (G6PDH2) and cellular growth rate?

1) Flux through G6PDH2 remains constant across all growth rates.   
2) Flux through G6PDH2 is negatively correlated with growth rate.   
3) Flux through G6PDH2 shows no statistically significant correlation with growth rate.   
4) Flux through G6PDH2 is positively correlated with growth rate.   
5) Flux through G6PDH2 increases at near-zero growth rates only.   
6) Flux through G6PDH2 decreases at both high and low growth rates, peaking at intermediate rates.   
7) Flux through G6PDH2 is inversely proportional to glucose uptake.
answer: The correct answer is 4) Flux through G6PDH2 is positively correlated with growth rate..

1) The presence of multiple gene copies encoding hydroxylamine oxidoreductase

Which of the following interventions has been demonstrated to increase the CD8+ T cell population and improve the effector to regulatory T cell ratio, thereby enhancing the efficacy of oxaliplatin and PD-1 blockade therapies in colorectal cancer?

1) Administration of Bifidobacterium breve JCM92

5) Delivery of Clostridium butyricum spores without encapsulation   
6) Supplementation with generic Lactobacillus species   
7) Inhibition of toll-like receptors on intestinal cells
answer: The correct answer is 1) Administration of Bifidobacterium breve JCM92.

Annotation and diversity assessment often rely on public genome repositories, metagenomic mapping, and the presence of essential single copy genes.

Which factor most likely contributed to the difficulty in functionally annotating the M. parvicella RN1 genome, despite high assembly completeness?

1) A lack of closely related reference genomes within public databases   
2) The use of long-read sequencing technologies instead of short paired-end reads   
3) High levels of contamination from non-bacterial DNA   
4) The absence of essential single copy genes in the assembly   
5) Overrepresentation of repetitive elements causing misassemblies   
6) Failure to submit sequence data to international repositories   
7) Use of automated annotation pipelines without any manual validation
answer: The correct answer is 1) A lack of closely related reference genomes within public databases.

Genome annotation and metabolic reconstruction The contigs were uploaded to the ‘MicroScope’annotation pipeline (Vallenet et al. , 2006, 2009) and automatic annotations were validated manually for the genes involved in metabolic pathways of interest. Comparison of the RN1 genome to full-scale community strains Metagenome data sets were previously generated from biomass from two wastewater treatment plants with enhanced biological phosphorus removal (EBPR), Aalborg East (Albertsen et al. , 2012) and Aalborg West (Albertsen et al. , in preparation: Data set uploaded to MG-RAST (Meyer et al. , 2008) ID: 4463936) WWTPs. Metagenome sequence readswere mapped to the genome of RN1 using CLC’smap reads to reference function, and requiring at least 70% similarity and a minimum read length of 50 bp. A three-dimensional recruitment plot wasconstructed, as described in Albertsen et al. (2012), to investigate the diversity among M. parvicella- related EBPR community strains. In addition,reads mapping at minimum 95% similarity were visualised using Circos (Krzywinski et al. , 2009) to investigate differences between the RN1 genomeand closely related community strains. Results and Discussion General features of the M. parvicella genome The genome of the M. parvicella RN1 strain that wasisolated from a conventional non-EBPR WWTPwas sequenced and partially assembled. The RN1 genome assembly is 4.2 Mbp divided into 87 contigs owing to repeat regions that could not be resolvedusing the PE insert length used in this study (Table 1 and Supplementary Figure S2). The presence of 106of the 107 selected ‘single copy essential genes’ (Dupont et al. , 2012) suggests that the genome is essentially complete (Supplementary Table S1). According to the integrated microbial genome(IMG) database (Markowitz et al. , 2012), the only absent gene at least also appears absent from genomes of some other organisms. Likewise, thethree genes present in duplicate are also found inmultiple copies in some genomes. Analysis of the genome revealed that more than 40% of the predicted coding sequences (CDS) hadno homologues to those found in other organisms, reflecting the lack of sequence information available for related organisms and Gram-positive bacteria ingeneral. In fact, the genome of the relatively distantly related Acidimicrobium ferrooxidans (see Supplementary Figure S1 for phylogeny) is the solerepresentative of the Acidimicrobidae actinobacter-ial subclass, of which M. parvicella is a member. Obtaining genome information for such under- represented phylogenetic groups is of additionalinterest, but also makes annotation of the selected pathways in the RN1 genome difficult, with rela- tively low levels of supporting evidence for somegenes. question:
Antarctic terrestrial environments host a remarkable diversity of bacterial phyla adapted to extreme cold, desiccation, and high UV radiation. Advances in genomics have revealed various strategies employed by these microbes to survive in such inhospitable conditions.

Which of the following is a genetic adaptation commonly found in Antarctic psychrophilic and psychrotolerant bacteria that enhances survival in cold environments?

1) Increased production of heat-shock proteins for high-temperature stability   
2) Accumulation of compatible solutes to prevent intracellular ice formation   
3) Development of endospores for long-term dormancy   
4) Utilization of sulfur-based energy metabolism   
5) Enhanced synthesis of chlorophyll for photosynthesis   
6) Thickening of cell walls to resist mechanical stress   
7) Reduction of membrane permeability to oxygen
answer: The correct answer is 2) Accumulation of compatible solutes to prevent intracellular ice formation.

Accurate quantification and identification of microbes require careful methodological choices and rigorous quality controls.

Which methodological step is critical for ensuring that fluorescence signals in qPCR originate from the intended PCR product rather than non-specific artifacts such as primer-dimers?

1) Using high molecular weight DNA extracted by CTAB/protein lysis   
2) Sequencing nearly full-length 16S rRNA genes   
3) Performing qPCR reactions in triplicate   
4) Analyzing melting curves after qPCR amplification   
5) Preparing DNA standards from cloned 16S rRNA genes   
6) Culturing isolates at low temperatures   
7) Selecting specific qPCR reagents and optimized conditions
answer: The correct answer is 4) Analyzing melting curves after qPCR amplification.

question:
Soil-dwelling Streptomyces bacteria interact with one another through the production of antibiotics, which serve as both offensive and defensive tools in microbial competition. These interactions are influenced by local environmental conditions and shape the evolution of both antibiotic production and resistance traits.

Which of the following outcomes is most likely if antibiotic resistance accumulates more rapidly than inhibitory phenotypes among Streptomyces populations in a nutrient-limited environment?

1) An unsustainable escalation of antibiotic production leading to continuous arms races   
2) Increased metabolic burden resulting in the collapse of Streptomyces populations   
3) A stable coexistence characterized by reduced selection for antibiotic producers   
4) The emergence of novel antibiotic compounds at an accelerated rate   
5) Complete exclusion of non-resistant species from the community   
6) A shift toward non-antibiotic-based competitive strategies such as resource partitioning   
7) Greater prevalence of broad-spectrum antibiotics due to intensified competition
answer: The correct answer is 6) A shift toward non-antibiotic-based competitive strategies such as resource partitioning.
text: that antibiotic inhibitory phenotypes are under significant local selection and mediate nutrient competition in local soil communities. However, the relatively greater accumulation of resistance than inhibitory phenotypes among Strep- tomyces isolates in natural habitats suggests that an escalating coevolutionary arms race may represent a cost-prohibitive trajectory for antibiotic-producers or that coevolutionary polymorphisms may be unba- lanced at best. The significant positive association of inhibition with nutrient overlap among locally coex- isting Streptomycetes suggests that antibiotics are likely to act as ‘weapons’ against sympatric compe- titors, but that coevolutionary displacement may provide a significant means for minimizing fitness costs of interspecies resource conflicts and the like- lihood of a coevolutionary arms race. This work sheds light on the roles of antibiotics in microbial interactions and coevolutionary dynamics within complex soil communities. However, because this study emphasizes inhibition and resistance among isolate pairs, these results are likely to underestimate both the complexity of Streptomycete coevolutionary dynamics and the potential outcomes of multispecies antibiotic inhi- bitory and resistance interactions in natural com- munities (Chait et al. , 2012). Deeper understanding of the diverse roles of antibiotics in species interac- tions in soil, the dynamics of antibiotic inhibition in natural habitats and especially the factors that may determine the potential for a coevolutionary arms race vs coevolutionary differentiation are crucial for understanding the long-term trajectories of antibio- tic-producing microbes in soil. Recent work suggests the potential for soil edaphic characteristics, nutri- ent availability or nutrient diversity in soil, physical environmental stress and phylogeny to predict microbial inhibitory activities and coevolutionary interactions in soil populations (Schlatter et al. , 2009; Bakker et al. , 2010; Kinkel et al. , 2011; Bailey and Kassen, 2012; Otto-Hanson et al. , 2013). More detailed understanding of the precise roles of these factors in mediating microbial species interactions and coevolution in soil will contribute significantly to the search for novel antibiotic biochemistries, to enhanced insight into the maintenance of antibiotic resistance genes in environmental microbes and to management of disease suppressive activity of indigenous soil microbes (Martinez et al. , 2011; Kinkel et al. , 2011; Kinkel et al. , 2012). The SOS response is a conserved bacterial regulatory system that is triggered by DNA damage and involves repressors such as LexA proteins to control the expression of DNA repair genes like recA. Some bacterial species may have multiple lexA genes, influencing the dynamics of SOS regulation and DNA damage adaptation.

Which statement best describes the functional consequence of having two distinct LexA proteins (LexA1 and LexA2) in Xanthomonas axonopodis pv. citri with respect to recA transcription and the SOS response compared to bacteria with only one lexA gene?

1) Both LexA1 and LexA2 together prevent any induction of recA after DNA damage, fully inhibiting the SOS response.   
2) The presence of LexA1 and LexA2 results in a decreased fold-induction of recA after DNA damage relative to single lexA systems.   
3) LexA2 primarily maintains low basal recA expression under normal conditions, while both LexA1 and LexA2 repress recA and allow dramatic induction upon DNA damage.   
4) LexA1 acts exclusively as an activator of recA, and LexA2 as a repressor, leading to constant high recA expression.   
5) Having two LexA proteins abolishes the need for recA in DNA repair by providing alternative repair mechanisms.   
6) Only LexA1 is functional, while LexA2 is a nonfunctional pseudogene with no effect on SOS regulation.   
7) The SOS response in Xanthomonas axonopodis pv. citri is not affected by DNA-damaging agents due to the redundancy of LexA proteins.
answer: The correct answer is 3) LexA2 primarily maintains low basal recA expression under normal conditions, while both LexA1 and LexA2 repress recA and allow dramatic induction upon DNA damage..

Genome sequencing and phylogenetic analyses are essential tools in understanding the diversity, ecological functions, and evolutionary relationships of bacterial species relevant to wastewater treatment processes. Tetrasphaera species, notable for their roles in enhanced biological phosphorus removal, exhibit distinct genetic and morphological features that impact their function in activated sludge systems.

Which of the following statements most accurately describes the phylogenetic placement of Tetrasphaera species based on genome sequence and 16S rRNA analysis?

1) T. elongata and T. japonica are both located in clade 1, while T. australiensis and T. jenkinsii are in clade 2.   
2) T. australiensis and T. jenkinsii are grouped together in clade 2, T. elongata is in clade 1, and T. japonica does not fall within any known clade.   
3) All four species are distributed evenly across clades 1 and 2.   
4) T. elongata, T. australiensis, and T. japonica are all found outside the major clades, while T. jenkinsii is in clade 1.   
5) T. japonica and T. jenkinsii share the same clade, separate from T. elongata and T. australiensis.   
6) Only T. elongata is placed in an established clade; the other three species are outside known clades.   
7) T. australiensis and T. elongata are both outside recognized clades, while T. japonica and T. jenkinsii are in clade 2.
answer: The correct answer is 2) T. australiensis and T. jenkinsii are grouped together in clade 2, T. elongata is in clade 1, and T. japonica does not fall within any known clade..

Mathematical models are frequently used to understand how the gut microbiome responds to perturbations such as antibiotic treatment. Choosing the appropriate level of model complexity can affect both interpretability and practical utility, especially in systems with limited available data.

When modeling the gut microbiome’s response to a short course of antibiotics, why might a simple, overdamped second-order differential equation be preferred over a detailed pairwise interaction model involving hundreds of species?

1) It enables modeling of oscillatory dynamics commonly seen after antibiotics.   
2) It allows for precise identification of all interspecies competitive relationships.   
3) It captures general recovery trends while remaining tractable with limited data.   
4) It eliminates the need to consider parameters like damping or restoring force.   
5) It ensures that diversity alone is always a sufficient metric for recovery.   
6) It predicts permanent loss of all microbial taxa after any disturbance.   
7) It requires less mathematical reparameterization compared to pairwise models.
answer: The correct answer is 3) It captures general recovery trends while remaining tractable with limited data..

Actinomycetes are a diverse group of gram-positive bacteria important in clinical microbiology both as rare opportunistic pathogens and as prolific sources of antibiotics. Understanding their laboratory characteristics and immune interactions is essential for accurate diagnosis and management.

1) Clearance of R. equi relies primarily on humoral immunity, while A. orientalis is a common human pathogen causing severe pneumonia.   
2) Both R. equi and A. orientalis are controlled by the same immune mechanisms, chiefly antibody-mediated responses.   
3) Clearance of R. equi depends on both CD4+ and CD8+ T-cell-mediated immunity, whereas A. orientalis is primarily known for antibiotic production and lacks established human pathogenicity.   
4) R. equi is best cleared by passive transfer of serum antibodies, and A. orientalis produces aminoglycoside antibiotics.   
5) Cellular immunity is unimportant in R. equi infection, and A. orientalis is frequently associated with clinical infections.   
6) Both organisms frequently infect immunocompetent hosts due to their resistance to T-cell-mediated immunity.   
7) Clearance of R. equi relies on neutrophil phagocytosis alone, and A. orientalis is a major cause of hospital-acquired infections.
answer: The correct answer is 3) Clearance of R. equi depends on both CD4+ and CD8+ T-cell-mediated immunity, whereas A. orientalis is primarily known for antibiotic production and lacks established human pathogenicity..

Probiotics are increasingly employed in swine production to promote growth, improve gut health, and enhance immune function in both piglets and sows. The efficacy of probiotic supplementation depends on multiple factors, including the strains used, timing, dosage, and whether both sows and offspring receive treatment.

Which scenario is most likely to maximize immune complement activity in piglets within a commercial swine operation?

1) Supplementing piglets only with Bacillus-based probiotics during post-weaning   
2) Administering high doses of L. rhamnosus exclusively to sows throughout gestation   
3) Providing moderate doses of L. plantarum and L. fermentum to piglets after weaning   
4) Supplementing both sows and piglets with a mixed probiotic containing multiple strains   
5) Giving L. fermentum to sows only during lactation   
6) Using only spore-forming Bacillus strains for piglets before weaning   
7) Administering probiotics to piglets at low doses during late gestation
answer: The correct answer is 4) Supplementing both sows and piglets with a mixed probiotic containing multiple strains.

Understanding the genomic and enzymatic features that enable this metabolic flexibility is crucial for appreciating their ecological roles in nutrient cycling.

Which combination of genomic features most directly enables a facultative anaerobe to both survive oxidative stress and perform complete denitrification under anoxic conditions?

1) Presence of catalase, superoxide dismutase, and nitrous oxide reductase genes   
2) Oxygen-dependent protoporphyrinogen oxidase, pyruvate dehydrogenase, and tetrathionate reductase genes   
3) Genes encoding multiple terminal oxidases, nitric oxide reductase, and dioxygenases   
4) Pyruvate dehydrogenase, 2-oxoglutarate dehydrogenase, and superoxide dismutase genes   
5) Catalase, superoxide dismutase, nitrite reductase, nitric oxide reductase, and nitrous oxide reductase genes   
6) Multiple membrane-bound oxidoreductases, dioxygenases, and catalase genes   
7) Respiratory nitrite reductase, polysulfide reductase, and catalase genes
answer: The correct answer is 5) Catalase, superoxide dismutase, nitrite reductase, nitric oxide reductase, and nitrous oxide reductase genes.

Variations in the methods used to generate these biomass equations can significantly impact the interpretation of core metabolic pathway activities, especially under different growth rates.

Which of the following statements most accurately describes how both ATP production and redox cofactor generation are affected as cellular growth rate decreases?

1) Glycolysis becomes increasingly responsible for both ATP and NADPH production at slower growth rates.   
2) The contribution of the TCA cycle to ATP production decreases while glycolytic ATP yield increases as growth slows.   
3) The Pentose Phosphate Pathway's role in NADPH generation diminishes significantly at low growth rates, with glycolysis taking over.   
4) TCA cycle and oxidative phosphorylation become more important for ATP production, while glycolysis's contribution declines; NADPH continues to be produced mainly via the Pentose Phosphate Pathway, with only minor changes in source contributions.   
5) Folate metabolism becomes the dominant source of NADPH at low growth rates, replacing the Pentose Phosphate Pathway.   
6) At slow growth, the majority of ATP and both redox cofactors are produced exclusively by glycolysis.   
7) NADPH yield increases and NADH yield decreases as growth rate decreases, with the TCA cycle providing most reducing equivalents.
answer: The correct answer is 4) TCA cycle and oxidative phosphorylation become more important for ATP production, while glycolysis's contribution declines; NADPH continues to be produced mainly via the Pentose Phosphate Pathway, with only minor changes in source contributions..

Streptomyces bacteria are prolific producers of antibiotics in soil environments, where they engage in complex interactions with other microbes. The evolution and maintenance of antibiotic resistance and production traits are shaped by both local adaptation and broader ecological and evolutionary dynamics.

Which factor most directly explains why resistance to antibiotics among Streptomyces isolates does not consistently show higher levels against sympatric (local) competitors compared to allopatric (non-local) ones?

1) High genetic recombination rates among Streptomyces populations   
2) Broad-spectrum resistance mechanisms such as multidrug efflux pumps   
3) Greater diversity of antibiotic compounds in allopatric environments   
4) Predominance of horizontal gene transfer from non-soil bacteria   
5) Uniform environmental conditions across different geographic locations   
6) Recent introduction of antibiotic-producing Streptomyces species   
7) Absence of metabolic cost associated with antibiotic resistance
answer: The correct answer is 2) Broad-spectrum resistance mechanisms such as multidrug efflux pumps.
text: provide compelling evidence for the significance of antibiotic inhibitory phenotypes to local interac- tions and Streptomyces fitness in soil. Resistance interactions among sympatric and allopatric isolate pairs In contrast to the inhibitory phenotypes, there was no consistent evidence among locations for the accumulation of resistance to locally coexisting isolates. Specifically, comparing the frequency of resistance to antibiotics produced by sympatric vs allopatric Streptomycetes , there was greater resis- tance to sympatric than allopatric isolates in four of the seven locations, and greater resistance to allopatric than sympatric isolates in three of the seven locations, although differences were statisti- cally significant in only two locations (data not shown). When data from all locations were com- bined, there was no significant difference in the frequencies of resistance to allopatric vs sympatric isolates (Figure 4). The apparent lack of locally adapted resistance suggests a number of possibilities about the evolutionary or coevolutionary dynamics of antibiotic inhibitory and resistance phenotypes within soil Streptomycete communities. Although one possible interpretation is that resistance does not confer a fitness benefit in local speciesinteractions, this seems unreasonable given the accumulation of resistance among Streptomycete isolates from all locations. Instead, the lack of locally adapted resistance may reflect different cost:benefit ratios of antibiotic production (high cost, high benefit) vs resistance (low cost, high benefit). Low fitness costs or a high frequency of compensatory mutations that reduce costs of resis- tance may lead to the retention of resistance in local habitats long after an antibiotic has been ‘lost’ from the population (Bottger et al. , 1998; Lenski and Riley, 2002; Luciani et al. , 2009; Brandis et al. , 2012; Dillon and Parti, 2012; Sousa et al. , 2012). Specifi- cally, although resistance phenotypes may be under strong local selection in the presence of a novel antibiotic, there may be a correspondingly rapid loss of antibiotic production capacity in the presence of high frequencies of resistance to that antibiotic. Novel antibiotic inhibitory phenotypes may be highly transient within populations (Cordero et al. , 2012), reflecting the metabolic dexterity of Strepto- myces (Tanaka and Omura, 1990; Challis and Hopwood, 2003), the high costs of antibiotic production (Williams and Vickers, 1986; although note Garbeva et al. , 2011) and the frequencies of local resistance. This may generate an unbalanced coevolutionary dynamic in which local adaptation of inhibitory phenotypes is stronger than local adaptation of resistance, as resistance against anti- biotics no longer produced by local competitors may be retained within the population. Consequently, evidence for local selection for resistance may be difficult to detect. General resistance mechanisms may also minimize the likelihood of locally adapted resistance. Finally, experimental constraints may further limit the detection of locally adapted resistance within Streptomycete populations. In particular, inhibition phenotypes were measured at a single time point and in simple pairwise combina- tions. 1) Ability to produce both lactate and succinate from glucose, with irreversibly acting lactate dehydrogenase

Probiotics and antimicrobial agents play key roles in promoting health, preventing infections, and ensuring food safety, especially through mechanisms like biofilm formation and pathogen inhibition. Understanding how specific bacterial traits and antimicrobial compounds interact is crucial in controlling both beneficial and harmful microbes in various environments.

Which of the following best explains why bacteriocin-producing lactic acid bacteria are valuable in reducing colonization by antibiotic-resistant pathogens in food environments?

1) They directly degrade antibiotics, neutralizing their effects on both pathogens and beneficial bacteria.   
2) They produce biofilms that uniformly enhance the growth of all microbes, including pathogens.   
3) They secrete natural antimicrobial peptides that inhibit the growth of drug-resistant bacteria.   
4) They increase the permeability of bacterial cell walls, making pathogens more susceptible to cleaning agents alone.   
5) They transform pathogenic bacteria into non-pathogenic forms through horizontal gene transfer.   
6) They exclusively adhere to stainless steel surfaces, preventing microbial transfer to foods.   
7) They induce mutations in pathogens that reduce their ability to form biofilms.
answer: The correct answer is 3) They secrete natural antimicrobial peptides that inhibit the growth of drug-resistant bacteria..

There are notable differences in OxyR function and gene regulation between Escherichia coli and Pseudomonas aeruginosa, both important gram-negative organisms.

Which feature most specifically distinguishes the OxyR-regulated oxidative stress response in Pseudomonas aeruginosa from that in Escherichia coli?

1) The requirement for OxyR to form a reversible intramolecular disulfide bond to become active   
2) The activation of DNA-binding proteins such as Dps during oxidative stress   
3) The presence of a unique OxyR-regulated gene, AhpB, not found in Escherichia coli   
4) The ability of both oxidized and reduced OxyR to bind DNA   
5) The recognition of a DNA motif consisting of four ATAG elements spaced at 10-base-pair intervals   
6) The induction of rpoS, a general stress response regulator, during oxidative stress   
7) The formation of OxyR homologs in other gram-negative bacteria
answer: The correct answer is 3) The presence of a unique OxyR-regulated gene, AhpB, not found in Escherichia coli.

5) Complete inability to form biofilms

Probiotics are live microorganisms that, when administered in adequate amounts, confer health benefits to their host. In aquaculture, the development and application of probiotics present unique challenges due to the aquatic environment's influence on host-microbe interactions.

Which of the following best explains why managing microbial communities in aquaculture hatcheries is particularly important compared to terrestrial animal husbandry?

1) Aquatic animals cannot inherit maternal microbiota and rely on environmental bacteria for initial colonization.   
2) Aquatic animals have digestive systems that are highly resistant to microbial colonization.   
3) Antibiotics are not effective against waterborne pathogens in aquaculture systems.   
4) Terrestrial animals are not exposed to environmental microbes post-birth.   
5) Water recirculation in aquaculture removes most bacteria from the environment.   
6) All aquatic animals possess a fully established gut microbiota at hatching.   
7) Probiotics are only effective in terrestrial animals due to stable microbiota.
answer: The correct answer is 1) Aquatic animals cannot inherit maternal microbiota and rely on environmental bacteria for initial colonization..

question:
Modifying titanium dioxide (TiO2) with various dopants and forming composite structures can significantly enhance its photocatalytic properties for applications such as hydrogen generation and pollutant degradation. Understanding the effects of different dopants, heterojunctions, and material phases is essential for designing efficient photocatalysts.

Which of the following strategies leads to the creation of an intermediate energy band that enables TiO2 to absorb visible light, thereby extending its photocatalytic activity beyond the ultraviolet range?

1) Codoping TiO2 with copper (Cu) and nitrogen

Effective probiotic development for poultry requires careful selection and validation of beneficial bacterial strains, often tailored to local conditions and host species.

Which approach is most likely to ensure that probiotic products are both effective and well-adapted for poultry production in a particular country such as Bangladesh?

2) Selecting lactic acid bacteria strains from dairy products used in human foods

4) Using genetically modified bacteria engineered for high growth rates

Bacterial biofilm formation is tightly regulated by intracellular signaling molecules and membrane-associated proteins that control the localization of surface adhesins. In Pseudomonas fluorescens, the interplay between c-di-GMP signaling, membrane receptors, and periplasmic proteases determines the stability of biofilms.

Which sequence of molecular events most accurately describes how phosphate starvation leads to biofilm dispersal in Pseudomonas fluorescens?

1) RapA expression increases, c-di-GMP levels rise, LapD binds c-di-GMP, LapG is inhibited, LapA remains on the surface.   
2) RapA is repressed, c-di-GMP accumulates, LapD does not bind c-di-GMP, LapG cleaves LapA, biofilm disperses.   
3) RapA expression increases, c-di-GMP decreases, LapD is free of c-di-GMP, LapG is active, LapA is cleaved and released.   
4) LapD loses the HAMP domain, c-di-GMP increases, LapA is not processed, biofilm disperses.   
5) Phosphate starvation causes LapG deletion, LapA accumulates on the surface, biofilm is reduced.   
6) c-di-GMP is hydrolyzed, LapD binds c-di-GMP, LapG is inhibited, LapA is released from the surface.   
7) LapA expression diminishes, c-di-GMP increases, LapG activity is unaffected, biofilm disperses.
answer: The correct answer is 3) RapA expression increases, c-di-GMP decreases, LapD is free of c-di-GMP, LapG is active, LapA is cleaved and released..

In a prior study, our group characterized LapD, reporting genetic and biochemical evidence that LapD binds c-di-GMP through its cytoplasmic EAL domain and controls biofilm formation via a periplasmic output domain [17]. The structure/ function analysis presented by Newell et al. suggested that LapDcontrols LapA localization by a unique inside-out signaling mechanism: binding c-di-GMP in the cytoplasm and transmitting this signal through the inner membrane to the periplasm via a HAMP domain. Such a mechanism could account for how changes in cytoplasmic c-di-GMP levels control LapA’s stability on the cell surface post-translationally. However, the mechanism by which LapD’s periplasmic domain impacted LapA localizationwas unknown. The availability of inorganic phosphate (Pi) is an important environmental signal that governs biofilm formation by P. fluorescens Pf0-1 via a c-di-GMP-dependent mechanism. When Pi is limiting, the c-di-GMP PDE RapA is expressed and depletes cellular c-di-GMP, suppressing biofilm formation [25]. One effect of RapA’s activity is the loss of the adhesin LapA from the cellsurface. While our previous study showed that the effects of Pistarvation and RapA expression on biofilm require signaling through LapD [17], the specific contribution of LapD to changes in LapA localization in this signaling pathway was not known. Here we uncover how LapD controls LapA localization and provide biochemical data describing its function as an inside-out signaling protein. When bound to c-di-GMP, LapD inhibits theactivity of a periplasmic protease, LapG. In the absence of c-di- GMP binding to LapD, LapG is free to cleave the N-terminus of LapA, releasing the adhesin from the cell and preventing biofilmformation. Upon Pi starvation, the LapD-LapG system responds to c-di-GMP depletion by RapA and promotes biofilm detachment. These data, in combination with the companion study by Navarroet al. [26] presenting a structural analysis of LapD’s signaling mechanism, describe a key connection in a complete c-di-GMP control circuit that links environmental signal to cellular output. 1) recA expression becomes constitutively high and unresponsive to DNA damage.   
2) recA expression is repressed below wild-type levels in response to DNA damage.

answer: The correct answer is 3) recA expression remains inducible by DNA damage, similar to wild-type cells..

question:
In bacterial genetics, gene disruption using antibiotic resistance markers and homologous recombination is a common method to study gene function. The ability of a plasmid to replicate in the host is a critical consideration when designing such experiments.

When disrupting a bacterial gene using a plasmid-borne antibiotic resistance cassette, which strategy ensures that only chromosomal integration events confer antibiotic resistance to the host?

1) Using a plasmid with an origin of replication functional in the host   
2) Employing a plasmid lacking an origin of replication recognized by the host   
3) Utilizing a plasmid carrying multiple antibiotic resistance markers   
4) Introducing the antibiotic resistance gene without flanking homologous sequences   
5) Selecting for spontaneous antibiotic resistance mutations in the host genome   
6) Using a temperature-sensitive plasmid that can replicate at all temperatures   
7) Cloning the gene of interest without any antibiotic resistance marker
answer: The correct answer is 2) Employing a plasmid lacking an origin of replication recognized by the host.

In soil microbial communities, competition for resources can drive the evolution of antibiotic production and resistance among coexisting species. The intensity and nature of these antagonistic interactions are influenced by local ecological factors such as nutrient availability and niche overlap.

Which scenario is most likely to result in strong antibiotic inhibition among soil Streptomycete populations?

1) Low nutrient niche overlap between sympatric isolates   
2) High nutrient niche overlap between allopatric isolates   
3) Low resource diversity with predominantly allopatric competitors   
4) High nutrient niche overlap among sympatric isolates   
5) High resource diversity and minimal antagonism   
6) Complete niche differentiation among coexisting species   
7) Low nutrient availability with allopatric populations
answer: The correct answer is 4) High nutrient niche overlap among sympatric isolates.

Among inhibitory isolate pairs, there was a significant positive correlation between niche overlap and the intensity of antibiotic inhibition among sympatric ( R¼0.29; P¼0.0013) but not allopatric isolate pairs ( R¼0.009; P¼0.478). Thus, isolates from the same location were better at inhibiting isolates with which they had large niche overlap than isolates with which they exhibited little niche overlap. In contrast, there was no relationship between niche overlap and the intensity of inhibition among Streptomycetes from different locations in soil, indicating that the niche-inhibitory phenotype relationship reflects local selection and not physiological tradeoffs. Local selection for inhibitory phenotypes is significantly related to niche overlap and presumably the inten- sity of competition between isolates from the same location in soil. The strength of this relationship varied and was not always significant within locations: among distinct locations, niche overlap explained from 7% to 60% of the total variation in inhibition zone sizes for sympatric isolate pairs within a location (for example, Figure 5). These data are consistent with the hypothesis that antibiotics mediate nutrient competition among Streptomycete populations within some local communities. However, the data also suggest that the significance of antibiotics to competitive interactions vary across the landscape, with communities ranging from those in which competition is ‘managed’ predominantly by niche differentiation to communities that are strongly antagonistic. This may reflect habitat variation (for example locations with little nutrient diversity and thus limited potential for niche differentiation may be most likely to support antagonistic interactions), or the evolutionary poten- tial of local populations. Perhaps most importantly, these data offer a distinct alternative to a coevolu- tionary arms race among interacting Streptomycetes . Manipulation of gut microbiota through dietary interventions is an important strategy in modern animal agriculture, particularly as alternatives to antibiotics are sought. Probiotics such as Enterococcus faecalis are evaluated for their ability to influence microbial communities and support animal health.

Which outcome most strongly indicates that Enterococcus faecalis supplementation can mimic the effects of antibiotics on pig gut microbiota composition?

1) Significant enrichment of Fibrobacteres in both E. faecalis and antibiotic groups   
2) Unique presence of 12 bacterial genera only in the basal diet group   
3) Comparable reduction in bacterial abundance and diversity between E. faecalis and antibiotic groups   
4) Dramatic increase in overall microbial diversity exclusively in the E. faecalis group   
5) Absence of lactic acid bacteria in pigs given E. faecalis   
6) Higher prevalence of 21 phyla only in antibiotic-treated pigs   
7) Greater abundance of fiber-digesting bacteria in probiotic-supplemented pigs compared to all other groups
answer: The correct answer is 3) Comparable reduction in bacterial abundance and diversity between E. faecalis and antibiotic groups.
text: Title: Microbial shifts in the porcine distal gut in response to diets supplemented with Enterococcus Faecalis as alternatives to antibiotics Year: 2017 Paper ID: b8e1717482bf33bbd9a43ddc9a1308ea6f21ac9a Abstract: Gut microbiota plays an important role in host health and nutrient digestion of animals. Probiotics have become one of effective alternatives to antibiotics enhancing animal health and performance through modulating gut microbiota. Previously, our research demonstrated that dietary Enterococcus Faecalis UC-100 substituting antibiotics enhanced growth and health of weaned pigs. To investigate the alterations of microbiota in the distal gut of pigs fed E. faecalis UC-100 substituting antibiotics, this study assessed fecal microbiota in pigs from different dietary treatments: the basal diet group, the E. faecalis group, and the antibiotic group on d 0, 14, and 28 of feeding through 16 S rRNA sequencing. Twenty-one phyla and 137 genera were shared by all pigs, whereas 12 genera were uniquely identified in the E. faecalis group on d 14 and 28. Bacterial abundance and diversity in the E. faecalis group, bacterial diversity in the antibiotic group, especially abundances of Fibrobacteres phylum and 12 genera in the E. faecalis group and antibiotics group were lower than that in the basal diet group on d 28. These results showed that microbial shifts in the porcine gut in response to diets containing E. faecalis were similar to the response to which containing antibiotics.
