question:
Melanized (dematiaceous) fungi are a diverse group of organisms with pigmented cell walls, capable of causing a range of diseases in humans. Their ecological adaptations and distribution significantly influence their pathogenic potential and epidemiology.

Which pairing of fungal genus and characteristic habitat or property is most accurately matched?

1) Scedosporium – exclusively found in saline coastal environments   
2) Exophiala – adapts to extreme environments and metabolizes xenobiotics   
3) Alternaria – primarily thrives in deep marine sediments   
4) Calosphaeriales – commonly isolated from arid desert soils   
5) Hortaea – prevalent in nitrogen-rich urban soils   
6) Rhinocladiella mackenziei – cosmopolitan distribution worldwide   
7) Pseudallescheria – restricted to cold alpine habitats
answer: The correct answer is 2) Exophiala – adapts to extreme environments and metabolizes xenobiotics.

We do notaim to review every publication regarding melanized fungi, butrather we seek to provide a broad, yet in-depth overview of theﬁeld as it currently stands, recognizing that it will continue to evolve and expand with our increasing knowledge of and ex-perience with these clinically important fungi. ECOLOGY Melanized or dematiaceous fungi as deﬁned above are fre- quently considered ubiquitous saprobes inhabiting living anddead plant material and, for the most part, residing in the soil.We now know, however, that these generalized assumptionsare incorrect for the group as a whole, as several etiologicagents occupy speciﬁc ecological niches or microenvironments,and the knowledge of their natural ecology contributes to ourunderstanding of their opportunistic/pathogenic potential(175, 177, 606, 779). It has been suggested (175) that our use ofthe term “dematiaceous” be restricted to those ubiquitous,mostly plant-associated hyphomycetous fungi with brown hy-phae (220, 221), such as Alternaria ,Bipolaris ,Curvularia , and Exserohilum in the order Pleosporales . The natural ecology of melanized fungi in several other orders is more restricted (187).For example, fungi in the order Calosphaeriales belong mostly to woody-plant- or wood-inhabiting genera such as Phaeoacremo- nium ,Phialemonium , and Pleurostomophora , whereas some gen- era in the order Chaetothyriales , such as Exophiala , may have speciﬁc microenvironments and are characterized as “micro-extremophiles.” The ability of some species in this genus, suchasE. xenobiotica , to grow in high concentrations of xenobiotics (606) such as xylene, toluene, or creosote-treated utility poles,as well as to cause human disease, is truly remarkable. Speciesin the genus Exophiala and related genera are frequently re- ferred to as the “black yeast-like fungi” and are so namedbecause of their ability to produce budding, yeast-like cells atsome point in their life cycle as well as dark hyphae. Theecology of Pseudallescheria andScedosporium was also recently investigated by examining the occurrence of these species innatural and human-dominated environments (393). Theseﬁndings demonstrated increasing environmental recovery withincreasing human habitation and a concomitant elevation innitrogen concentrations. Another genus deﬁned by its resi-dence in a particular environmental niche is the halophilicgenus Hortaea in the order Capnodiales .Hortaea werneckii , the agent of tinea nigra, is found in subtropical saltwater habitatsand is manifested by its opportunistic adherence to the dead,salty keratin layers of the human hand (87). Thus, while severalgenera are considered “ubiquitous,” many prefer well-deﬁnedmicroenvironments which, for some genera, predispose themto causing disease where similar conditions exist in the host. In addition, there are species that appear to be geographi- cally restricted, such as Rhinocladiella mackenziei , which has been seen primarily in patients from the Middle East (726).While Scedosporium proliﬁcans has been reported from many locations, most clinical cases originate from Australia andSpain, for unclear reasons (76, 336). Understanding their mechanisms and efficacy is crucial as the industry seeks alternatives to antibiotic use.

Which of the following statements best explains the primary mechanism by which early administration of competitive exclusion (CE) products reduces colonization of pathogenic bacteria in chicks?

1) CE products directly kill pathogenic bacteria through antimicrobial compounds.   
2) CE products neutralize bacterial toxins via enzymatic degradation.   
3) CE products stimulate the chicks' immune system to produce specific antibodies.   
4) CE products populate the gut with beneficial microbes that outcompete pathogens for resources and niches.   
5) CE products alter the genetic makeup of pathogens, rendering them non-virulent.   
6) CE products increase gut acidity, making the environment hostile to all bacteria.

answer: The correct answer is 4) CE products populate the gut with beneficial microbes that outcompete pathogens for resources and niches..

2) Alkyl hydroperoxide reductase (ahpF)

5) Mini-ferritin (dps)   
6) Electron transfer flavoprotein (fixA)   
7) Drug efflux protein (TolC)
answer: The correct answer is 5) Mini-ferritin (dps).

Key proteins such as LapD, LapG, and associated domains coordinate to control the localization and activity of the cell surface adhesin LapA.

1) High c-di-GMP binding to LapD, recruitment of LapG to the inner membrane, and LapA retention   
2) Activation of the Pho regulon, RapA-mediated c-di-GMP depletion, LapD inactivation, and free LapG activity   
3) Mutations disabling the HAMP domain of LapD, increased LapD-LapG interaction, and LapA accumulation   
4) Elevated environmental phosphate, Pho regulon repression, and LapG sequestration by LapD   
5) Overexpression of LapD with functional EAL domain, high c-di-GMP, and LapG inhibition   
6) Inactive RapA, high c-di-GMP, and LapG tethered to inner membrane   
7) Deletion of LapG, constitutive Pho regulon activity, and LapA cleavage
answer: The correct answer is 2) Activation of the Pho regulon, RapA-mediated c-di-GMP depletion, LapD inactivation, and free LapG activity.

question:
Probiotics, particularly lactic acid bacteria (LAB), are increasingly used in poultry production to enhance gut health and reduce reliance on antibiotics. The effectiveness of a candidate probiotic strain depends on its ability to persist in the gastrointestinal tract, inhibit pathogens, and interact favorably with the host.

Which characteristic is essential for a lactic acid bacterium to be considered an effective probiotic for poultry, as it directly facilitates colonization of the gut and exclusion of harmful pathogens?

1) Production of hydrogen peroxide   
2) β-Galactosidase enzyme activity   
3) High resistance to heat during feed processing   
4) Strong adhesion to gut epithelial cells   
5) Production of volatile fatty acids   
6) Ability to form endospores   
7) Utilization of complex polysaccharides
answer: The correct answer is 4) Strong adhesion to gut epithelial cells.
text: RESEARCH ARTICLE Open Access Isolation, characterization, and assessment of lactic acid bacteria toward their selection as poultry probiotics Rine Christopher Reuben1,2, Pravas Chandra Roy1, Shovon Lal Sarkar1, Rubayet-Ul Alam1and Iqbal Kabir Jahid1* Abstract Background: Probiotics are live microorganisms that, when administered in adequate amounts, confer a health benefit on the host, are now accepted as suitable alternatives to antibiotics in the control of animal infections and improving animal production. Lactic acid bacteria (LAB) with remarkable functional properties have been evaluated in different studies as possible probiotic candidates. The purpose of this study was to isolate, characterize and assess the potentials of LAB from poultry gastrointestinal tract as potential poultry probiotics. Results: Potential LAB probiotics were isolated from broilers, characterized and evaluated for probiotic properties including antagonistic activity (against Escherichia coli ,E. coli O157: H7, Enterococcus faecalis ,Salmonella Typhimurium, S.Enteritidis and Listeria monocytogenes ), survivability in simulated gastric juice, tolerance to phenol and bile salts, adhesion to ileum epithelial cells, auto and co-aggregation, hydrophobicity, α–glucosidase inhibitory activity, and antibiotic susceptibility tests. Most promising LAB strains with excellent probiotic potentials were identified by API 50 CHL and 16S rRNA sequencing as Lactobacillus reuteri I2,Pediococcus acidilactici I5,P. acidilactici I8,P. acidilactici c3,P. pentosaceus I13, and Enterococcus faecium c14. They inhibited all the pathogens tested with zones of inhibition ranging from 12.5 ± 0.71 to 20 ± 0 mm, and competitively excluded ( P< 0.05) the pathogens examined while adhering to ileum epithelial cells with viable counts of 3.0 to 6.0 Log CFU/ml. The selected LAB strains also showed significant ( P< 0.005) auto and co-aggregation abilities with α-glucosidase inhibitory activity ranging from 12.5 to 92.0%. The antibiotic susceptibility test showed 100.00% resistance of the LAB strains to oxacillin, with multiple antibiotic resistance indices above 0.5. Conclusion: The selected LAB strains are ideal probiotic candidates which can be applied in the field for the improvement of poultry performance and control of pathogens in poultry, hence curtailing further transmission to humans. 1) Rely exclusively on traditional sequence homology searches using Arr as a template   
2) Perform functional screening assays to detect ADP-ribosylation activity in mutant strains

6) Detect ribosomal protein synthesis rates as an indirect marker

Which of the following practices is most critical to ensure the effective use of probiotics for improving fish larval survival in hatcheries?

1) Routinely applying broad-spectrum antibiotics alongside probiotics   
2) Selecting probiotic strains based on their demonstrated in vivo efficacy and host specificity   
3) Relying solely on laboratory (in vitro) screening of bacterial strains   
4) Introducing any available lactic acid bacteria without prior testing   
5) Enriching live feed organisms with uncharacterized environmental microbes   
6) Focusing only on water quality parameters and ignoring microbial communities   
7) Using pathogenic bacteria to stimulate immune development in larvae
answer: The correct answer is 2) Selecting probiotic strains based on their demonstrated in vivo efficacy and host specificity.

1) Applying DFT with no U corrections and fixed symmetry constraints, using only the Gamma-point   
2) Using DFT+U with U applied to Ti 3d and Cu 3d states, no U on O 2p, and enforcing non-spin-polarized calculations   
3) Applying DFT+U with U = 4.5 eV for Ti 3d, U = 7 eV for Cu 3d, and additional U correction for O 2p states, allowing spin polarization and no symmetry constraints   
4) Utilizing standard DFT with U applied only to Cu 3d states and keeping the structure undistorted   
5) Performing DFT calculations at multiple k-points with U applied to all elements except oxygen, enforcing symmetry constraints

7) Employing DFT without any U corrections but including a Hubbard correction on hydrogen
answer: The correct answer is 3) Applying DFT+U with U = 4.5 eV for Ti 3d, U = 7 eV for Cu 3d, and additional U correction for O 2p states, allowing spin polarization and no symmetry constraints.

2) LexA1 and LexA2 only regulate homologous recombination genes, so their loss affects only MMC resistance.   
3) MMS directly inactivates LexA1 and LexA2, allowing constitutive SOS gene expression regardless of genotype.

The use of natural, biological agents for controlling microbial contamination is increasingly important in the food industry. Lactic acid bacteria (LAB) and their biofilms are being explored as alternatives to chemical disinfectants for improving food safety.

Which characteristic is essential for probiotic LAB strains intended for biocontrol applications in food processing environments to ensure both safety and efficacy?

1) Production of gelatinase enzymes for biofilm degradation   
2) Ability to tolerate low pH and bile salts   
3) Resistance to all commonly used antibiotics   
4) Presence of virulence genes for competitive advantage   
5) Inhibition of only non-pathogenic bacteria   
6) Reduced aggregation capability to avoid clumping   
7) Sensitivity to conventional biocides
answer: The correct answer is 2) Ability to tolerate low pH and bile salts.

7) Undoped TiO₂ with high surface roughness

The cell envelope of Gram-negative bacteria is a complex, multilayered structure critical for maintaining cellular integrity, mediating environmental interactions, and supporting survival under various stress conditions. The protein composition of this envelope can impact bacterial virulence, resistance mechanisms, and adaptation to host environments.

Which feature uniquely distinguishes the outer membrane of Gram-negative bacteria from the inner membrane and periplasmic space, contributing to both structural integrity and defense against host immune factors?

1) Presence of a thick peptidoglycan layer   
2) Abundance of porin proteins   
3) Localization of lipopolysaccharide (LPS) in the outer leaflet   
4) High concentration of cytoplasmic enzymes   
5) Exclusive housing of efflux pumps   
6) Attachment of fimbrial structures   
7) Incorporation of phospholipids only
answer: The correct answer is 3) Localization of lipopolysaccharide (LPS) in the outer leaflet.
text: 2011 ). The survival of A. actinomycetemcomitans in these disparate environments is dependent on the protein composition of the cell envelope. The cell envelope of this and other Gram- negative bacteria is comprised of three layers: an inner membrane adjacent to the cytoplasm, a periplasmic space containing the cell wall, and an outer membrane separating the periplasm from the extracellular environment. Both membranes are composed of a phospholipid bilayer containing peripheral and integral membrane proteins with the outer membrane forming an asymmetric bilayer due to the incorporation of lipopolysaccharide (LPS) in the outer leaflet ( Silhavy et al. 2010 ). The cell envelope, as a whole, is a critical structure involved in maintaining cellular homeostasis ( Silhavy et al. 2010 ). This equilibrium is maintained by the dynamic interaction between the compartments of the cell. These interactions are mediated by individual proteins or protein complexes that allow for the transport of macromolecules between the cytoplasm and the external milieu or to be incorporated into the envelope itself. Therefore, the cell envelope can be viewed as a single unit inclusive of proteins found in both membranes, the periplasmic space, and peripherally associated with the inner membrane. The nature of the proteins that comprise the cell envelope will be dependent on the cellular environment. However, a proportion of proteins or protein orthologs will be present in the envelope of most, if not all, Gram-negative bacteria. Despite the importance of these proteins, few envelope proteins have been characterized in A. actinomycetemcomitans. In this work, we used a gel-free mass spectrometry approach to detect proteins present in whole membrane fractions of VT1169, an afimbriated serotype b strain of A. actinomycetemcomitans . A total of 648 unique proteins were consistently identified. Bioinformatic analyses indicate that these proteins have diverse functions including virulence determinants, secretion, transport, metabolism, and energy generation. In addition, 107 proteins in the dataset were identified which have not been characterized. Which combination of protein secretion systems is found in Aggregatibacter actinomycetemcomitans, distinguishing it from some closely related species?

1) Type I, II, III, and V secretion systems   
2) Type I, II, IV, and V secretion systems   
3) Type II, III, IV, and VI secretion systems   
4) Type I, II, and V secretion systems only   
5) Type III, IV, and VI secretion systems only   
6) Type II, V, and VI secretion systems only   
7) Type I, III, and VI secretion systems only
answer: The correct answer is 4) Type I, II, and V secretion systems only.

question:
Essential oils are complex mixtures of volatile compounds derived from plants, widely valued for their bioactive properties including antimicrobial, antioxidant, and immunomodulatory effects. Their application is being explored in both health and food industries, particularly as natural alternatives to synthetic chemicals and antibiotics.

Which property of essential oils is most directly attributed to their phenolic components and is notably effective at concentrations of 0.01–10 mg/mL in cell models?

1) Inhibition of viral replication   
2) Disruption of microbial cell membranes   
3) Promotion of cytokine secretion   
4) Enhancement of gut microbial diversity   
5) Neutralization of free radicals   
6) Stimulation of hormone production   
7) Acceleration of cell proliferation
answer: The correct answer is 5) Neutralization of free radicals.
text: Title: Antimicrobial, Antioxidant, and Immunomodulatory Properties of Essential Oils: A Systematic Review Year: 2019 Paper ID: 78fe6ee4c881b2663449c292fb1e5251e4e7dbad Abstract: Essential oils (EOs) are a mixture of natural, volatile, and aromatic compounds obtained from plants. In recent years, several studies have shown that some of their benefits can be attributed to their antimicrobial, antioxidant, anti-inflammatory, and also immunomodulatory properties. Therefore, EOs have been proposed as a natural alternative to antibiotics or for use in combination with antibiotics against multidrug-resistant bacteria in animal feed and food preservation. Most of the results come from in vitro and in vivo studies; however, very little is known about their use in clinical studies. A systematic and comprehensive literature search was conducted in PubMed, Embase®, and Scopus from December 2014 to April 2019 using different combinations of the following keywords: essential oils, volatile oils, antimicrobial, antioxidant, immunomodulation, and microbiota. Some EOs have demonstrated their efficacy against several foodborne pathogens in vitro and model food systems; namely, the inhibition of S. aureus, V. cholerae, and C. albicans has been observed. EOs have shown remarkable antioxidant activities when used at a dose range of 0.01 to 10 mg/mL in cell models, which can be attributed to their richness in phenolic compounds. Moreover, selected EOs exhibit immunomodulatory activities that have been mainly attributed to their ability to modify the secretion of cytokines.

question:
Lactic acid bacteria such as Oenococcus oeni and Lactobacillus species are essential for malolactic fermentation in winemaking, a process that not only softens wine acidity but also enhances its flavor stability. The adaptation of these bacteria to challenging wine environments involves complex physiological and metabolic responses to stressors like ethanol and acid.

Which mechanism specifically aids Oenococcus oeni in maintaining plasma membrane integrity during ethanol stress encountered in winemaking environments?

1) Activation of citrate lyase for diacetyl production   
2) Accumulation of lactobacillic acid in the plasma membrane   
3) Increased secretion of exopolysaccharides   
4) Enhanced malic acid uptake via malate permease   
5) Production of hydrogen peroxide as a stress signal   
6) Downregulation of ATPase activity   
7) Formation of endospores to survive harsh conditions
answer: The correct answer is 2) Accumulation of lactobacillic acid in the plasma membrane.

1) γH2AX and 53BP1 form large, overlapping foci that directly colocalize with viral genomes within the first 6 hours post-infection.   
2) ATM kinase is robustly phosphorylated at Ser1981 and relocates into prominent nuclear foci early after HCMV infection.   
3) 53BP1 foci dramatically increase in number and intensity specifically at viral replication centers early after infection.   
4) γH2AX and 53BP1 foci in infected cells are larger and brighter than in mock cells, but these foci are juxtaposed, not directly overlapping with viral genomes.   
5) Early after HCMV infection, ATM and phosphorylated ATM are both relocalized to sites of viral genome deposition.

Which methodological step is essential to ensure DNA quality and reliability of downstream molecular analyses when studying bacterial diversity in low-biomass Antarctic soils?

1) Immediate freezing of samples at ambient temperature   
2) Extraction of DNA without cell disruption   
3) Quantification and purity assessment of extracted DNA   
4) Use of non-specific primers in qPCR assays   
5) Sampling from sites with frequent human disturbance   
6) Omission of technical replicates during sampling   
7) Storage of samples at room temperature for extended periods
answer: The correct answer is 3) Quantification and purity assessment of extracted DNA.

Accurate identification of dematiaceous fungi is essential in clinical settings due to their role in opportunistic infections among immunocompromised patients.

Which statement best explains why molecular techniques, such as DNA sequencing, have become the gold standard for identifying species within genera like Exophiala and Scedosporium?

1) Morphological features of these fungi are sufficient for distinguishing all clinically relevant species.   
2) Many species within these genera lack sexual reproductive forms, making traditional methods unreliable.   
3) Synanamorphs in these genera cannot be cultured in laboratory conditions.   
4) DNA sequencing has revealed that what appeared to be single species are actually complexes of several genetically distinct species.   
5) All dematiaceous fungi are resistant to antifungal treatments, regardless of identification method.   
6) The ITS region is unsuitable for differentiating between species in these genera.   
7) Homothallic reproduction is absent in all clinically relevant species of Exophiala and Scedosporium.
answer: The correct answer is 4) DNA sequencing has revealed that what appeared to be single species are actually complexes of several genetically distinct species..

The advent of sequencing characterization has provided the tools necessaryto reevaluate the evolutionary relationships of these blackmolds, and today multilocus molecular phylogenetic studiesare clearly redeﬁning previously described entities, uncoveringnew species and varieties, and correlating these with theirnatural habitats. IDENTIFICATION OF ETIOLOGIC AGENTS Over 150 species and 70 genera of dematiaceous fungi have been implicated in human and animal disease (Table 2). As thenumber of patients immunocompromised as a result of dis-eases and medical therapy increases, additional species arebeing reported as causes of human disease, expanding an al-ready long list of potential pathogens. Identiﬁcation of mela-nized etiologic agents known to cause human or animal diseasehas traditionally been based upon phenotypic features of theisolate observed in culture (175, 177, 220, 221). This practicecontinues to be the mainstay of fungal identiﬁcation in mostroutine settings. More recently, molecular techniques em-ployed for classiﬁcation purposes and those provided by re-search facilities have provided additional tools for the charac-terization of these molds. Extensive sequencing for somegenera has illustrated the concept of “species complexes,” orthe inclusion of several separate species into what was formerlyreferred to as a single species. This has been clearly demon-strated in the genera Exophiala (825), Scedosporium (281–283), and Phaeoacremonium (525). The “splitting” of these species into separate taxa has of necessity changed our reporting prac-tices. As an example, laboratories previously comfortable withdiscriminating only between Exophiala (Wangiella )dermatitidis and E. jeanselmei are now aware of several other clinically signiﬁcant species that are not easily separated by phenotypicfeatures alone (177, 184, 825) and that E. jeanselmei is in fact one of the less frequent agents of disease. Therefore, speciesother than E. dermatitidis are best reported as an Exophiala sp., notE. dermatitidis , unless sequencing has provided a species identiﬁcation. These “new and improved” reporting tech-niques, however, must be communicated to clinicians in a man-ner consistent with their understanding of current organismterminology and the associated mycoses. question:
Colorectal cancer is among the most prevalent and deadly cancers worldwide. Its development and progression are influenced by a complex interaction of genetic, environmental, immune, and microbial factors, with recent therapies targeting the gut microbiome to improve patient outcomes.

Which of the following mechanisms most directly links gut microbiota dysbiosis to increased colorectal cancer risk?

1) Enhanced synthesis of protective short-chain fatty acids by beneficial bacteria   
2) Reduction in oncogenic mutations due to improved immune surveillance   
3) Activation of carcinogenic pathways and promotion of DNA damage by increased pathogenic bacteria   
4) Increased diversity of gut microbes leading to stable intestinal barriers   
5) Uptake of dietary fiber leading to decreased microbial activity   
6) Suppression of antitumor responses through increased physical activity   
7) Genetic mutations in APC, KRAS, and p53 genes independent of microbial influence
answer: The correct answer is 3) Activation of carcinogenic pathways and promotion of DNA damage by increased pathogenic bacteria.
text: from a 2020 survey by the World Health Organization, CRC ranks third and second in terms of incidence and mortality among all cancers and third and second in terms of incidence among men and women, respectively (Sung et al., 2021). The latest data show that the number of new cases of Frontiers in Microbiology 01 frontiersin.org fmicb-13-945533 August 4, 2022 Time: 6:44 # 2 Chen et al. 10.3389/fmicb.2022.945533 CRC in the world is as high as 193 million in 2020, and it is expected that the number of new cases of CRC in the world will increase to 2.5 million by 2035, surpassing common cancers such as liver cancer and gastric cancer (Sung et al., 2021). The evolution of CRC is a complex multistep process. With the continuous developments and changes in people’s lifestyles toward Western lifestyles, the incidence and mortality rates of CRC are rising (Chen W. et al., 2016), which seriously threatens human health. The pathogenesis of CRC is complex and is due to synergistic eﬀects of multiple factors. Its risk of occurrence is not only associated with mutations in multiple genes but also depends on the immune status of the patient, which is positively correlated with the intestinal ﬂora. In recent years, with the intensiﬁcation of research on intestinal microorganisms, research on the use of immunotherapy for treating CRC has been widely carried out in clinical settings. Further research on gut microbiota is likely to provide a promising approach for improving the eﬃcacy of existing chemotherapy drugs, reducing their toxicity, and improving the sensitivity of immunotherapy (Gopalakrishnan et al., 2018). Gut microbiota promote intestinal repair by promoting cell proliferation and diﬀerentiation, which are essential for maintaining the integrity of the intestinal barrier (Krishnan et al., 2015). There is growing evidence that the large and complex gut microbiota interact via a complex mechanism with substances in the surrounding microenvironment (Geller et al., 2017). Gut microbiota play a critical role not only in maintaining the homeostasis of the intestinal environment but also in the maturation and sustainable development of the immune system (Thaiss et al., 2016). Various factors such as age, diet, lifestyle, and genotype act synergistically to cause changes in the structure and abundance of intestinal microbial populations (Seesaha et al., 2020). Imbalances in gut microbiota and disorders of ﬂora population structure such as reductions in populations of beneﬁcial bacteria and the presence of Clostridium, Enterobacter, and other pathogenic bacteria result in microecological imbalances and thereby disrupt cell DNA, activate carcinogenic signaling pathways, and ultimately aﬀect the development of CRC (Brennan and Garrett, 2016; Figure 1). In recent years, fecal microbiota transplantation has improved the beneﬁts of treatment for patients with many diseases (Lu et al., 2019). Fecal microbiota transplantation involves the transfer of fecal microbiota from a healthy donor to the patient’s intestine to correct bacterial imbalances and restore intestinal homeostasis. Mycobacterium smegmatis employs various genetic strategies to survive antibiotic exposure and environmental stress, including the expression of specific resistance genes. The arr gene, encoding an ADP-ribosyltransferase, plays a critical role in conferring rifampin resistance and is regulated by global transcriptional factors.

Which of the following best explains why a Δarr (arr deletion) strain of Mycobacterium smegmatis remains unaffected in growth and general stress responses but displays increased sensitivity to rifampin?

1) arr is essential for cell wall biosynthesis, but redundant pathways compensate for its loss under stress.   
2) arr only functions during stationary phase, so its deletion impacts cells only under starvation.   
3) arr is a global regulator of stress response genes, so its deletion is lethal unless complemented.   
4) arr specifically modifies rifampin via ADP-ribosylation, conferring resistance without affecting general stress adaptation.   
5) arr deletion leads to upregulation of alternative antibiotic resistance mechanisms.   
6) arr encodes a transporter that effluxes a broad range of toxic compounds except rifampin.   
7) arr deletion disrupts DNA repair pathways essential for survival under antibiotic stress.
answer: The correct answer is 4) arr specifically modifies rifampin via ADP-ribosylation, conferring resistance without affecting general stress adaptation..

Which combination of factors most directly determines the extent to which orally ingested nanoparticles are absorbed into systemic circulation and influence their distribution to organs such as the liver and spleen?

1) Size, surface area, aggregation state, and dissolution rate of the nanoparticles   
2) Flavor additives and packaging materials of food products   
3) The host’s age and gender only   
4) The specific antimicrobial coating used, independent of other properties   
5) The presence of silicon dioxide and titanium dioxide in cosmetics alone   
6) The nanoparticles' ability to generate heat within the gut environment   
7) The time of day oral exposure occurs, without considering nanoparticle properties
answer: The correct answer is 1) Size, surface area, aggregation state, and dissolution rate of the nanoparticles.

The impact of nanoparticles on the host microbiota in the gastrointestinal tract is believed to play a key role in the outcome of any given therapy. Nanoparticles were proved to exhibit preferential damage on the microbiota but, also, it is believed that microorganisms of normal microbiota could inﬂuence toxicity of nanoparticles and their interaction with the host cells on site [ 7]. Although oral administration of functional nanoparticles is not a common event, nanoparticles come in contact with human microbiota very often through ingestion of solid food, water, cosmetics, and personal care products. Nanoparticles are contained as active ingredients by numerous cosmetic and daily care products, and their interaction with human microbiota is unavoidable. Among these, Ag, SiO 2, TiO 2, and ZnO nanoparticles are most relevant for oral ingestion because they are added as ingredients to food and many are contained in healthcare products. Numerous aspects, such as physicochemical properties, particle size, surface area, particle number, aggregation/agglomeration state, charge, and surface coatings are all likely to inﬂuence the biological effects and action mechanisms of orally-administered nanoparticles [ 68]. Moreover, oxidant generation and rate of dissolution were proved to impact the absorption of nanoparticles at the gastrointestinal level; therefore, these mechanisms are considered when investigating gastrointestinal drug delivery nanoparticles. Although not fully demonstrated, researchers consider that the mechanisms of action and impact of nanoparticles on the components of the gastrointestinal tract can vary due to resident microbial species, strain, diet, housing conditions, time of dosing, circadian rhythm variations, and endogenous microbiota [ 2]. These elements could also impact on the efﬁciency of functional nanoparticles in the treatment of gastrointestinal diseases, including infections. 4.2.1. Absorption After reaching the gastrointestinal tract, nanoparticles can be translocated through the intestinal barrier in a multistep process that involves diffusion through the mucus layer, contact with enterocytes and/or M-cells, and uptake via cellular entry or paracellular transport. The most common mechanism for uptake of NP into intestinal epithelial cells appears to be endocytosis with various mechanisms, such as clathrin-mediated, caveolae-mediated, clathrin and caveolae-independent, and macropinocytosis [ 69]. The uptake mechanism seems to be inﬂuenced by the physicochemical properties of the nanoparticles, their aggregative behavior, and size [70]. Studies have demonstrated that non-lymphoid areas can also be involved in the absorption of nanoparticles, particularly with conjugation of nutrients or nutrient-like compounds, which may increase their uptake. question:
Probiotic supplementation in livestock, particularly in pigs, is being explored as an alternative to antibiotics due to concerns over resistance and regulatory restrictions. Analyzing how such probiotics influence gut microbial diversity is essential for understanding their potential benefits in animal health and growth.

Which of the following outcomes most strongly supports the hypothesis that Enterococcus faecalis UC-100 supplementation modulates pig gut microbiota in a beneficial manner, comparable to antibiotic use?

1) Increased number of operational taxonomic units (OTUs) unique to the E. faecalis UC-100 group at certain time points   
2) Decreased total DNA sequencing data collected from fecal samples   
3) Reduction in the number of microbial species present in all diet groups   
4) Consistently lower feed-to-gain ratios in the basal diet group compared to the probiotic group   
5) Complete absence of diarrhea in pigs fed only a basal diet   
6) No difference in microbial community composition between any dietary groups   
7) Lower OTU diversity in the E. faecalis UC-100 group compared to the antibiotic group
answer: The correct answer is 1) Increased number of operational taxonomic units (OTUs) unique to the E. faecalis UC-100 group at certain time points.

question:
The human gut microbiome is shaped by a variety of intrinsic and extrinsic factors and plays a vital role in health and disease. Advances in sequencing and bioinformatics have enabled comprehensive taxonomic and functional profiling of gut microbial communities.

Which of the following approaches allows for both taxonomic identification and direct functional inference of microbial communities in fecal samples by sequencing all genetic material present?

1) 16S rRNA amplicon sequencing   
2) Shotgun metagenomic sequencing   
3) Metaproteomics   
4) Quantitative PCR   
5) Fluorescence in situ hybridization (FISH)   
6) Sanger sequencing of cultured isolates   
7) Single-cell genomics
answer: The correct answer is 2) Shotgun metagenomic sequencing.

Additionally, geography, life style, age, certain diseases and drug usage can all affect the gut microbial composition and function [2,33]. The distribution of microbes along the gastrointestinal (GI) tract is non-random, in that, certain species of microbes are co-localizing. Lactobacillacea ,Veilonellaceae and Helicobacterceae co-occur in stomach, Bacillaceae and Streptococcaceae in the small intestine, and Bacteroidaceae ,Clostridium , Lactobacillaceae and Biﬁdobacterium in the colon [ 34]. Dysbiosis in the intestinal ecosystem has been both directly and indirectly linked to autoimmune diseases (e.g., type 1 diabetes (T1D), rheumatoid arthritis (RA)) [ 35,36], colon cancer [ 37], type 2 diabetes (T2D) and obesity [ 5,25], cardiovascular disorders [ 38], non-alcoholic fatty liver disease (NAFLD) [39,40] as well as inﬂammatory bowel disease (IDB) [41]. 3. Gut Microbiome Proﬁling and Functional Annotation Metagenomics shotgun sequencing [ 42] and 16S rRNA amplicon sequencing [ 43] have been used for proﬁling gut microbiota from fecal (stool) samples. An appropriately annotated shotgun metagenomics dataset can be used for accurately mapping and predicting microbiota-affected metabolic pathways. These approaches also have proven potential for novel gene discovery [ 44] and identiﬁcation of essential functions. Annotation of metagenomics datasets is primarily carried out in two ways: (a) by assembling nucleotide sequences from NGS reads of appropriate length and subsequently predicting the protein coding sequences (called CDS) [ 45], and (b) by mapping the reads to genome or non-redundant marker gene sets of the relevant organisms guided by the taxonomic proﬁling [ 46]. These genes can be clustered, catalogued and aligned against reference database(s) of annotated gene/protein families (e.g., KEGG Orthology [ 47]), and/or they can be linked to metabolic pathways (e.g., MetaCyc [48]). Various computational tools and pipelines have been developed for these sorts of purposes. MOCAT2, for example, provides automated annotation of non-redundant reference catalogues from 18 databases covering various functional categories [ 45]. HMP Unified Metabolic Analysis Network (HUMAnN2) is a pipeline for profiling the relative abundances of microbes and the activity of their metabolic pathways from metagenomics data [ 46,49]. MEtaGenome ANalyzer (MEGAN) is an interactive and comprehensive microbiome analysis toolbox, that allows researchers to explore and analyze large-scale metagenomics datasets both from taxonomic and functional perspectives [ 50]. Metagenomics Rast (MG-RAST), is a RAST (Rapid Annotation using Subsystem Technology) server for automated annotation of metagenomics datasets [ 51]. Integrated Microbial Genomes & Microbiomes (IMG/M) is another server-based system that supports the annotation and analysis of microbiome datasets [ 52]. There is a plethora of tools for sequence assembly , gene prediction and phylogenetic classification which underpin many of these processes, and these tools are extensively reviewed elsewhere [53]. Functional annotation of metagenomics datasets poses several challenges in itself [ 53,54]. Although metagenomics data categorizes microbial functions at the community level, it fails to suggest a mechanistic explanation for how these functions arise. question:
Melanized (dematiaceous) fungi are a diverse group of darkly pigmented molds capable of causing a variety of infections, especially in immunocompromised individuals. These infections can present diagnostic and therapeutic challenges due to overlapping clinical features and intrinsic antifungal resistance.

Which of the following characteristics best explains the increased resistance of melanized fungi to environmental stress and certain antifungal agents?

1) Production of extracellular polysaccharide capsules   
2) Presence of thick, non-pigmented cell walls   
3) Synthesis of melanin within the fungal cell wall   
4) Exclusive intracellular replication   
5) Dependence on obligate parasitism   
6) Formation of non-septate hyphae   
7) Absence of ergosterol in the cell membrane
answer: The correct answer is 3) Synthesis of melanin within the fungal cell wall.

1) It increased both microbial diversity and abundance relative to pigs on a basal diet.   
2) It had no significant effect on either microbial diversity or abundance.   
3) It reduced microbial diversity and abundance, likely due to bacteriocin-mediated inhibition of other microbes.   
4) It caused a significant shift in β-diversity, altering the overall community structure.   
5) It resulted in an increase in Fibrobacteres abundance exclusively.   
6) It eliminated the dominance of Firmicutes and Bacteroidetes in the gut microbiome.   
7) It enhanced the proliferation of pathogenic bacteria in the gut.
answer: The correct answer is 3) It reduced microbial diversity and abundance, likely due to bacteriocin-mediated inhibition of other microbes..

These adaptations enable survival, metabolism, and ecological success in polar, deep-sea, and permafrost habitats.

Which of the following adaptations specifically helps cold-adapted bacteria maintain membrane fluidity and function during sudden temperature drops?

1) Accumulation of trehalose for cryoprotection   
2) Upregulation of carotenoid biosynthesis for oxidative stress resistance   
3) Production of exopolysaccharides to form biofilms   
4) Modification of peptidoglycan composition in the cell wall   
5) Synthesis of cold shock proteins for nucleic acid stabilization   
6) Activity of fatty acid desaturases increasing unsaturated membrane lipids   
7) Expression of capA and acspA genes for cold acclimation proteins
answer: The correct answer is 6) Activity of fatty acid desaturases increasing unsaturated membrane lipids.

question:
DNA repair in bacteria involves multiple pathways that respond to ultraviolet (UV) radiation-induced damage, including photoreactivation, nucleotide excision repair, and mutagenic DNA repair systems. The interplay between these systems determines both bacterial survival and mutation rates in environments with fluctuating light exposure.

Which of the following statements best describes the primary role of the rulAB determinant in Pseudomonas species under UV stress?

1) It encodes a photolyase that directly repairs cyclobutane pyrimidine dimers using visible light.   
2) It enhances the binding of UvrABC excision nuclease to DNA lesions.   
3) It encodes an error-prone DNA polymerase that confers UV tolerance by allowing mutagenic DNA repair.   
4) It completely suppresses the mutation rate during UV exposure.   
5) It provides no survival advantage in UV-sensitive mutants lacking nucleotide excision repair.   
6) It acts exclusively during photoreactivation and has no effect in the absence of light.   
7) It is only present on the bacterial chromosome and not on plasmids.
answer: The correct answer is 3) It encodes an error-prone DNA polymerase that confers UV tolerance by allowing mutagenic DNA repair..

Certain anaerobic bacteria display unique metabolic adaptations for carbon fixation and energy generation. Ignavibacterium album showcases distinct enzymatic features compared to green sulfur bacteria, particularly in the reverse TCA cycle and electron transport mechanisms.

Which combination of features distinguishes Ignavibacterium album from typical green sulfur bacteria engaged in autotrophic CO₂ fixation?

1) Presence of the glyoxylate cycle and ubiquinone biosynthesis genes   
2) Reliance on ATP-dependent citrate lyase for citrate cleavage and absence of menaquinone-7 production   
3) Possession of ATP-independent citrate lyase genes, lack of ATP-dependent citrate lyase, absence of ubiquinone biosynthesis, and production of menaquinone-7   
4) Complete set of glyoxylate cycle enzymes and multiple ATP-dependent citrate lyase isoforms   
5) Utilization of the Calvin-Benson cycle for carbon fixation and exclusive use of cytochrome oxidase for respiration   
6) Absence of any ferredoxin proteins and exclusive aerobic lifestyle   
7) Presence of both ATP-dependent and ATP-independent citrate lyase enzymes, with ubiquinone as the primary electron carrier
answer: The correct answer is 3) Possession of ATP-independent citrate lyase genes, lack of ATP-dependent citrate lyase, absence of ubiquinone biosynthesis, and production of menaquinone-7.

Because the glyoxylate cycle is not present, PFOR is probably essential for the assimilation ofacetate by carboxylation of acetyl-CoA to pyruvate. Unlike its GSBrelatives, the I. album genome does not encode ATP-dependent citrate lyase, which is a key enzyme required for autotrophicCO 2ﬁxation by the reverse TCA cycle in GSB ( Wahlund and Tabita, 1997 ). The genes for alternative enzymes found in other organisms with reverse TCA cycle activity, namely citryl-CoAsynthetase and citryl-CoA lyase ( Aoshima et al., 2004a,b ), and the postulated type II ATP-dependent citrate lyase ( Hügler and Sievert, 2011 ), were also absent. However, the I. album genome does include genes (IALB_1146, IALB_1147) that encode an ATP-independent citrate lyase ( Bott and Dimroth, 1994 ). IALB_1146 encodes the αsubunit, CitF, while IALB_1147 encodes a fusion of theβandγsubunits, CitE and CitD. This enzyme catalyzes the cleavage of citrate to acetate and oxaloacetate, and it is involvedin citrate fermentation in some organisms ( Meyer et al., 2001 ). It is possible that this enzyme performs the same function inI. album . In support of this possibility, a putative citrate trans- porter gene (IALB_1014) occurs in the genome. Although thisrole has not yet been proposed for this enzyme, an interestingpossibility that must be considered is that the ATP-independentcitrate lyase could also function in the reverse TCA cycle in I. album . If so, this organism would then possess a complete reverse TCA cycle. The operation of the reverse TCA cycle for CO 2 assimilation would also depend upon the availability of electronsources to produce reduced ferredoxin. The genome of I. album includes genes necessary to take advantage of some potential elec-tron sources and for the production of reduced ferredoxin fromthem (see below). In conclusion, the gene content of the I. album genome shows that the organism can probably grow mixotroph-ically. Additionally, it may hav e a complete but unconventional reverse TCA cycle ( Figure 4 ), but this hypothesis will have to be tested experimentally. 1) Chemically modified metals   
2) Synthetic polymers   
3) Natural products from plants and microorganisms   
4) Radiation-based therapies   
5) Genetically engineered viruses   
6) Engineered nanoparticles   
7) Recombinant antibodies
answer: The correct answer is 3) Natural products from plants and microorganisms.

Which approach enables researchers to reconstruct human muscle cell metabolic networks to identify potential biomarkers for diabetes by integrating protein abundance and gene expression data?

Lactic acid bacteria (LAB) are widely recognized for their role in forming biofilms that can inhibit the growth of pathogenic microorganisms in food processing environments. Their antimicrobial effects rely on various mechanisms, making them promising agents for food safety and probiotic-based cleaning applications.

Which combination of mechanisms most directly contributes to the effectiveness of LAB biofilms in reducing pathogenic bacterial contamination on food contact surfaces?

1) Bacteriocin production, biosurfactant secretion, and pathogen exclusion via biofilm trapping and killing   
2) Antibiotic synthesis, spore formation, and increased pathogen motility   
3) Enhanced oxygen tolerance, hydrogen sulfide production, and iron scavenging   
4) Genetic recombination with pathogens, toxin inactivation, and plastic degradation   
5) UV radiation resistance, endospore lysis, and rapid fermentation   
6) Chitinase secretion, volatile organic compound emission, and silicon uptake   
7) Lignin degradation, nitrate fixation, and mycotoxin production
answer: The correct answer is 1) Bacteriocin production, biosurfactant secretion, and pathogen exclusion via biofilm trapping and killing.
text: can be attributed to a combination of factors like biosurfactant and bacteriocin production as well as mechanisms of pathogens exclusion through their trapping (killing of cells embedded in bioﬁlms). This is in accordance with previous works like Guerrieri et al. (2009) witch suggests the need to apply the bacteriocine-producing microorganism, in bioﬁlms. There may be an inﬂuence of EPS (exo-polysaccharide). Kim et al. (2006) found that the EPS of Lactobacillus acidophilus A4 had stronger anti-bioﬁlm activity against the growth of entero-hemorrhagic E. coli O157: H7, S. enteritidis ,S. typhimurium KKCCM 11806, Yersinia enterocolitica ,Pseudomonas aeruginosa KCCM 11321, Listeria monocytogenes Scott A, and B. cereus . CONCLUSION Our results show that LAB strains from foods can be excellent candidates to form protective bioﬁlms, in accordance with the hypothesis proposed by Falagas and Makris (2009) to use non-pathogenic microorganisms, namely probiotics, as part of daily cleaning products to lower the incidence of pathogenic microorganisms. Evidences on the eﬃcacy of probiotics for the prevention and treatment of infections have been observed both in vitro and in vivo (Levkovich et al., 2013; Shu et al., 2013). The present study provided new information about the use of potential probiotic LAB bioﬁlms for the control of Listeria monocytogenes ,S.Typhimurium and E. coli O157:H7 bioﬁlms formation through exclusion mechanisms. However, more experiments are needed to conﬁrm the ability of these strains to inhibit the pathogen bioﬁlm formation in other environments. Our initial studies are very encouraging and indicate that the LAB that we have tested are promising candidates for controlling the presence of pathogenic bioﬁlms in food-processing facilities. The development of protective bioﬁlms with probiotic LAB present in food could help avoiding problems of contamination into the food chain. Strategies to improve the biological relevance of these models include incorporating experimental data and simulating temporal changes in metabolite concentrations.

Which approach most effectively enables a genome-scale metabolic model to account for the carryover of specific metabolites between distinct growth phases in batch or fed-batch cultures?

1) Increasing the number of reactions for each metabolic pathway in every phase   
2) Randomly assigning flux values to key metabolites at phase boundaries   
3) Adding accumulation reactions that transfer experimentally-verified metabolites from one phase to the next   
4) Deleting all non-essential reactions at the end of each phase   
5) Using only steady-state fluxes for all metabolites regardless of phase   
6) Disabling all demand reactions except for biomass during transitions   
7) Assigning fixed rates for all metabolites based solely on theoretical predictions
answer: The correct answer is 3) Adding accumulation reactions that transfer experimentally-verified metabolites from one phase to the next.

question:
Dental implants are susceptible to biofilm-related infections, which can compromise implant function and longevity. Various strategies have been developed to prevent microbial colonization and biofilm maturation on implant surfaces.

Which of the following statements accurately characterizes the advantages and limitations of localized antibiotic delivery systems for dental implants?

1) They prevent biofilm formation without affecting implant properties but contribute to antibiotic resistance with prolonged use.   
2) They eliminate the risk of antibiotic resistance by minimizing systemic exposure.   
3) They only target mature biofilms and are ineffective against early colonizers.   
4) They require systemic administration to achieve therapeutic effects at the implant site.   
5) They universally disrupt the oral microbiome, leading to cytotoxicity in host tissues.   
6) They render silver coatings obsolete due to superior antimicrobial potency and safety.   
7) They permanently prevent all forms of bacterial colonization on implant surfaces.
answer: The correct answer is 1) They prevent biofilm formation without affecting implant properties but contribute to antibiotic resistance with prolonged use..

Antibiotic coatings, on the other hand, have some drawbacks, the most signiﬁcant of which are related to antibiotic resistance. The process of bioﬁlm formation starts with salivary glycoproteins developing a conditioning ﬁlm (also known as the acquired enamel pellicle) on the teeth surface, which allows initial bacterial adherence [ 34]. After that process, weak long-distance forces between charged molecules of the pellicle and the pioneer bacterial species will grant initial adhesion. These forces grow stronger via receptor pairs between adhesins in the bacteria’s surface and glycoprotein receptors in the acquired pellicle [ 34]. After the initial adhesion, bioﬁlm development continues with cell aggregation until a stable microcolony is achieved. At last, due to multiple factors such as lack of nutrient or ﬂuid dynamics, bioﬁlm can disperse from the surface of the implant and migrate to other areas or tissues [64]. Medical devices, among others dental titanium implants, show a process of bioﬁlm formation quite similar to natural teeth. A titanium surface, when present in the oral cavity, is immediately coated by plasma and saliva proteins. This will result in the formation of a protein layer that allows initial colonizers, such as various species of Streptococcus , to bind to it. Co-aggregation follows and interactions by different species induce bioﬁlm accumulation. Finally, the extracellular matrix starts embedding microbial communities, and the bioﬁlm is established [65]. 1,3,5-Triazine derivatives are valuable compounds in medicinal chemistry due to their diverse biological activities and versatility in chemical modification. The controlled substitution of cyanuric chloride's chlorine atoms with various nucleophiles allows for systematic exploration of new drug candidates.

Which combination of factors is essential for the selective mono- and disubstitution of cyanuric chloride with N-nucleophiles to synthesize 1,3,5-triazine derivatives with confirmed structures?

1) Controlled reaction temperature, presence of sodium carbonate, stepwise nucleophile addition, and structural confirmation using NMR, IR spectroscopy, and elemental analysis   
2) Use of transition metal catalysts, high-pressure conditions, and mass spectrometry alone for structure determination   
3) Acidic reaction medium, simultaneous addition of all nucleophiles, and UV-Vis spectroscopy for structural analysis   
4) Microwave irradiation, water as the only solvent, and reliance solely on melting point determination   
5) Excess nucleophile, uncontrolled heating, and in situ FTIR monitoring without further analysis   
6) Photochemical activation, basic alumina as catalyst, and refractive index measurement for structure confirmation   
7) Enzymatic catalysis, anaerobic conditions, and gas chromatography-mass spectrometry as the primary characterization tool
answer: The correct answer is 1) Controlled reaction temperature, presence of sodium carbonate, stepwise nucleophile addition, and structural confirmation using NMR, IR spectroscopy, and elemental analysis.

question:
Molecular diagnostic assays are increasingly used to detect bacterial pathogens in clinical and food safety settings, replacing traditional culture techniques due to their speed and specificity. Detecting Mycobacterium avium subsp. paratuberculosis (MAP) is critical in managing Johne’s disease and ensuring dairy safety.

Which methodological approach ensures high specificity in a PCR-based assay for detecting MAP amidst closely related mycobacteria and diverse bacterial backgrounds?

1) Targeting the multi-copy IS900 sequence present in several mycobacterial species   
2) Using universal 16S rRNA gene primers for broad bacterial detection   
3) Employing the single-copy F57 genomic sequence unique to MAP as the assay target   
4) Omitting internal controls to minimize assay complexity   
5) Relying solely on phenotypic culture characteristics   
6) Incorporating primers that amplify conserved regions among all mycobacteria   
7) Testing only reference strains without including clinical or environmental isolates
answer: The correct answer is 3) Employing the single-copy F57 genomic sequence unique to MAP as the assay target.

question:
Bacterial survival under oxidative stress depends on complex defense strategies that neutralize reactive oxygen intermediates (ROIs) and repair oxidative damage. Key regulatory proteins and enzymes coordinate these responses to maintain cellular integrity during both normal metabolism and acute oxidative challenges.

Which of the following best explains why Pseudomonas aeruginosa can effectively survive in environments with fluctuating oxidative stress?

1) It lacks superoxide dismutase but has enhanced DNA repair enzymes.   
2) It produces a single catalase enzyme with broad specificity.   
3) Its oxidative stress defense genes are constitutively expressed at all times.   
4) It possesses multiple isoforms of antioxidant enzymes and regulates their expression in response to oxidative conditions.   
5) It relies exclusively on iron sequestration to prevent hydroxyl radical formation.   
6) It uses SoxR to regulate catalase expression in response to hydrogen peroxide.   
7) It depends only on free radical scavengers for protection against ROIs.
answer: The correct answer is 4) It possesses multiple isoforms of antioxidant enzymes and regulates their expression in response to oxidative conditions..

Mycobacterium avium subsp. paratuberculosis (MAP) is a bacterial pathogen of major concern in animal and human health, especially due to its transmission through foods of animal origin such as milk. Molecular detection of MAP requires assays that can distinguish it from related environmental mycobacteria to ensure accurate diagnosis and food safety.

1) 16S rRNA gene   
2) IS900 element   
3) hsp65 gene   
4) F57 sequence   
5) rpoB gene   
6) IS1311 element   
7) ITS region
answer: The correct answer is 4) F57 sequence.

question:
Open data sharing and clearly defined contributor roles have become essential practices in computational biology, enabling transparency, reproducibility, and collaborative research. These standards are particularly important in large-scale projects involving metabolic modeling and industrial biotechnology applications.

Which combination of practices best demonstrates a commitment to transparency, reproducibility, and open science in computational biology research?

1) Making both computational models and analysis code publicly available along with a detailed breakdown of individual author contributions   
2) Publishing research findings in a closed-access journal and restricting code access to collaborators   
3) Providing only summary results without sharing underlying data or code   
4) Listing all authors alphabetically without specifying individual roles or responsibilities   
5) Depositing experimental data in a proprietary database with limited access   
6) Citing previous work without offering any new tools or open resources   
7) Releasing only the final manuscript without supplementary materials or contributor information
answer: The correct answer is 1) Making both computational models and analysis code publicly available along with a detailed breakdown of individual author contributions.

The gastrointestinal (GI) tract is a complex environment where interactions between microbes and the immune system play critical roles in both health and disease, including metabolic disorders. Innate immune receptors such as TLRs and NLRs are central to detecting microbial and danger signals, influencing inflammation and metabolism.

Which combination correctly matches the pattern recognition receptor with its typical cellular location and a microbial component it recognizes?

1) TLRs—cell cytosol—recognize peptidoglycan   
2) NLRs—cell surface—recognize flagellin   
3) TLRs—endo-lysosomal compartments and cell surface—recognize lipopolysaccharide   
4) NLRs—cell membrane—recognize LPS   
5) TLRs—nucleus—recognize DAMPs   
6) NLRs—lysosomes—recognize viral RNA   
7) TLRs—mitochondria—recognize peptidoglycan
answer: The correct answer is 3) TLRs—endo-lysosomal compartments and cell surface—recognize lipopolysaccharide.

Microbes interact with host cells: immunity links microbes to metabolism Different systems recognise and monitor the presence of micro- organisms in the body. For example, in the gastrointestinal tract (GI), epithelial cells play a major role as guardians that trans-late key information to the immune cells located in the lamina propria. In fact, the recognition and the monitoring of microbes is mainly performed by the innate immune system with pattern recognition receptors (PRRs) such as toll-like receptors (TLRs) and NOD-like receptors (NLR). 19 The TLRs are transmembrane receptors expressed on cell surfaces (ie, TLR-2, 4, 5) or in endo-lysosomal compartments (ie, TLR-3, 7, 8, 9 or 13), whereas NOD receptors are cytosolic proteins. Together, these recep- tors recognise pathogen-associated molecular patterns (PAMPs) from microorganisms (eg, lipopolysaccharides, peptidoglycans, lipoteichoic acid, flagellin and muramyldipeptide) or danger-as-sociated molecular patterns from damaged tissues. 19 Thus, the GI tract not only contains a vast majority of the microbes that reside in the human body but also harbours probably the larger pool of the immune cells that are present in the body.20 Notably, the immune system also has a predominant effect on the compo-sition of the microbiota. 21 Therefore, GI cells are continually exposed to a vast number of microbial antigens and metabolites. In spite of this close proximity, we live with microorganisms in perfect symbiosis (figure 2). question:
Titanium implants are frequently used in dental and orthopedic applications due to their mechanical strength and biocompatibility, but their surfaces are prone to bacterial colonization and infection. Which combination of surface modification strategies most directly targets both the prevention of bacterial biofilm formation and the promotion of osteoblast activity on titanium implants?

1) Doping titanium with bismuth and applying only organic silane coatings   
2) Utilizing silver nanoparticles and omitting any osteogenic biopolymer layers   
3) Incorporating drug-loaded coatings with antibiotics and leaving the surface unmodified otherwise

5) Employing layer-by-layer assembly of antimicrobial agents combined with chitosan/alginate multilayers   
6) Using gold-silver nanocages exclusively for photothermal therapy without additional coatings   
7) Relying solely on mechanical roughening to increase bone integration
answer: The correct answer is 5) Employing layer-by-layer assembly of antimicrobial agents combined with chitosan/alginate multilayers.

Which of the following is most characteristic of allergic bronchopulmonary aspergillosis (ABPA) but not of allergic bronchopulmonary mycosis (ABPM) due to non-Aspergillus fungi?

1) Presence of asthma   
2) Marked peripheral eosinophilia   
3) Elevated total serum IgE   
4) Positive skin test to fungal allergens   
5) Proximal bronchiectasis on imaging   
6) Excellent response to systemic corticosteroids   
7) Occurrence in immunocompetent individuals
answer: The correct answer is 5) Proximal bronchiectasis on imaging.

Relatively few fungi are re-sponsible for the majority of infections. (i) Onychomycosis. Dematiaceous fungi are rare causes of onychomycosis. Clinical features may include a history oftrauma, involvement of only one or two toenails, and lackof response to standard systemic therapy (316). Alternaria , Scopulariopsis , and Neoscytalidium have been reported, with the last genus being highly resistant to therapy (68, 316, 643,752). In one study, Neoscytalidium infection was associated with plucking of green tea leaves (68). Itraconazole andterbinaﬁne are the most commonly used systemic agents andmay be combined with topical therapy for refractory cases(316, 752). No published data are available for the newerazole agents. (ii) Tinea nigra. Tinea nigra is an uncommon infection con- ﬁned to the stratum corneum. The characteristic appearance isthat of a pigmented macule, usually on the palms or soles, andmay be bilateral (440, 682). It is usually asymptomatic. Themost common reported cause is Hortaea werneckii (previously Phaeoannellomyces werneckii ), with some cases due to Stenella araguata (87, 588, 682). Most cases are associated with expo- sure to sandy beaches in tropical regions, where H. werneckii is found in areas of high salinity (588). However, individual casesdue to Scopulariopsis brevicaulis ,Phoma eupyrena , and Chaeto- mium globosum with ﬁndings consistent with tinea nigra have also been reported (57, 154, 287). Diagnosis is made by skinscraping, and biopsy is not needed. Although systemic antifun-gals have been given with success (318), topical therapy withazoles or keratolytics is very effective (87, 588). Deep local infections. Deep local infections are a heteroge- nous group of infectious syndromes that are typically caused by local trauma. Virtually any of the melanized fungi discussed inthis review may cause these infections. question:
In the development of antimicrobial-producing bacterial strains for use in agriculture or food production, ensuring both efficacy and safety is essential. This involves sophisticated screening, survival optimization, and careful management to prevent unintended consequences such as resistance.

Which step is fundamental for confirming that a candidate bacterial strain does not pose a risk of spreading antibiotic resistance or causing disease in its intended host?

1) Assessing the strain's ability to survive passage through the gastrointestinal tract   
2) Evaluating the strain’s tolerance to industrial processing conditions   
3) Rotating antimicrobial agents during treatment protocols   
4) Conducting comprehensive genomic analysis to detect pathogenicity and resistance genes   
5) Encapsulating the strain to enhance viability post-administration   
6) Monitoring the animal’s microbiota composition for personalized interventions   
7) Combining the strain with prebiotic compounds to improve efficacy
answer: The correct answer is 4) Conducting comprehensive genomic analysis to detect pathogenicity and resistance genes.
text: A thorough genetic characterization of candidate strains i s essential in order to conﬁrm the safety of the bacterial stra in and ensure the lack of virulence and antibiotic resistance gen es. The chosen molecule or strain must be able to stay active in the host and withstand industrial treatments. One must also keep in mind that the GI tract is a highly complex environment with numerous bacterial species that can aﬀect the eﬃcacy of these antimicrobials, perhaps in a diﬀerent manner from one animal to another. Moreover, C. perfringens and other bacteria are highly adaptable micro-organisms. It is thus of high importance to develop and use products in a rational manner in order to avoid the appearance of strains resistant to these novel antimicrobials, as has occurred with convention al antibiotics. question:
Microbial communities in permafrost environments are increasingly important to both climate science and astrobiology. The study of extremophilic bacteria from these habitats reveals adaptations that could have significant ecological and technological implications.

Which statement best explains why extremophilic bacteria such as Planococcus halocryophilus Or1 are considered valuable models for astrobiological research on planets like Mars or moons such as Enceladus?

1) They can photosynthesize efficiently at low light levels found in icy environments.   
2) Their ability to metabolize sulfur compounds mirrors potential Martian biochemistry.   
3) Their cold-adapted enzymes and osmotic stress tolerance suggest mechanisms for microbial survival in subzero brines.   
4) They produce methane exclusively through non-biological chemical processes.   
5) Their membrane lipids function optimally only at high temperatures.   
6) They are the primary source of Earth's permafrost greenhouse gas emissions.   
7) Their genetic material is identical to microbes found in Antarctic glaciers.
answer: The correct answer is 3) Their cold-adapted enzymes and osmotic stress tolerance suggest mechanisms for microbial survival in subzero brines..
text: indicating that these cryoenviron- ments harbor active microbial ecosystems. Given that permafrost represents B26% of Earth’s soil ecosystem and undergoing rapid melting with globalwarming, microbial activity could release the large carbon reservoir as CO 2and CH 4, even at subzero temperatures. Extremophiles such as P . halocryophilus Or1 will expand our insights into molecular traits required for subzero growth and provide a modelfor understanding how biomolecules function in viable and dividing bacterial cells at the coldest growth temperatures described to date. Cold-activeand osmotically stable enzymes or metabolitesfrom P . halocryophilus Or1 carry high interest for future investigations. Lastly, as the search for evidence of life continues in our solar system,organisms such as P . halocryophilus Or1 provide an analog of how life can function in subzero brines; being one of the possible liquid water habitatsthought to exist on Mars (McEwan et al. , 2011) and other solar system targets including Enceladus (Postberg et al. , 2011). Which of the following antifungal agents is noted for its effectiveness against recalcitrant or resistant infections caused by dematiaceous molds in immunocompromised patients?

1) Amphotericin B   
2) Fluconazole   
3) Caspofungin   
4) Terbinafine   
5) Voriconazole   
6) Micafungin   
7) Flucytosine
answer: The correct answer is 4) Terbinafine.

Which definition most accurately describes a prebiotic as recognized by current expert consensus in microbiology and nutrition science?

1) A compound that directly kills harmful gut bacteria   
2) A live microorganism that confers a health benefit on the host   
3) A substrate selectively utilized by host microorganisms to confer a health benefit   
4) A dietary supplement that provides essential vitamins and minerals   
5) A medication that modulates immune responses in the gut   
6) A genetic sequence associated with improved metabolic outcomes   
7) A metabolite produced by gut bacteria that increases blood glucose levels
answer: The correct answer is 3) A substrate selectively utilized by host microorganisms to confer a health benefit.

Pseudomonas aeruginosa is a Gram-negative bacterium renowned for its adaptability and resistance to hostile environments, including the oxidative stress imposed by host immune defenses. The bacterium employs intricate gene regulation systems to detoxify reactive oxygen species and repair DNA damage.

Which scenario most clearly demonstrates the essential, non-redundant role of the OxyR protein in oxidative stress defense in Pseudomonas aeruginosa?

1) An OxyR-deficient mutant exhibits hypersensitivity to hydrogen peroxide despite normal levels of catalase KatA.   
2) A recG mutant displays high sensitivity to UV irradiation but normal resistance to organic peroxides.   
3) Overexpression of katB leads to modest increases in hydrogen peroxide tolerance, even in the absence of OxyR.   
4) Deleting the entire oxyR-recG operon causes only a minor reduction in survival following oxidative stress.   
5) A wild-type strain fails to upregulate ahpB in response to paraquat exposure.   
6) KatA expression is dramatically upregulated after exposure to organic peroxides in an OxyR mutant.   
7) Constitutive activation of the oxyR-recG promoter in wild-type cells leads to decreased DNA repair efficiency.
answer: The correct answer is 1) An OxyR-deficient mutant exhibits hypersensitivity to hydrogen peroxide despite normal levels of catalase KatA..

Transcription of these genes was regulated in response to H2O2, paraquat, or organic peroxides. Expression of katB-lacZ and the observed KatB catalase levels in P. aeruginosa PAO1 were induced up to 250-fold after exposure to oxidative stress-generating compounds. Also, ahpB-lacZ and ahpC-lacZ expression was 90- and 3-fold higher, respectively, upon exposure to paraquat. The dose- and time-response curves revealed that 1 mM paraquat was sufﬁcient for half-maximal activation of each reporter fusion within 5 min of exposure. Expression of these genes was not observed in a DoxyR mutant, indicating that OxyR was essential for this response. The transcriptional start sites of katB-ankB ,ahpB , and ahpC-ahpF were mapped, putative OxyR-binding sites were identiﬁed upstream of the 235 promoter elements, and direct binding of puriﬁed OxyR protein to these target promoters was demonstrated. The oxyR mutant was hyper- susceptible to oxidative stress-generating agents, including H2O2and paraquat, in spite of total KatA catalase activity being comparable to that of the wild type. The oxyR phenotype was fully complemented by a plasmid containing the oxyR gene, while any of the katB ,ahpB ,o r ahpCF genes alone resulted in only marginal complementation. Increased katB-lacZ expression and higher KatB catalase levels were detected in a DahpCF background compared to wild-type bacteria, suggesting a compensatory function for KatB in the absence ofAhpCF. In P. aeruginosa ,oxyR is located upstream of recG , encoding a putative DNA repair enzyme. oxyR-lacZ and recG-lacZ reporter activities and oxyR-recG mRNA analysis showed that oxyR and recG are organized in an operon and expressed constitutively with regard to oxidative stress from a single promoter upstream of oxyR . Mutants affected in recG but not oxyR were dramatically impaired in DNA damage repair as measured by sensitivity to UV irradiation. In conclusion, we present evidence that the oxyR-recG locus is essential for oxidative stress defense and for DNA repair. Which of the following statements most accurately describes a major concern regarding the therapeutic use of nanoparticles in relation to the gut microbiome?

1) Nanoparticles exclusively target pathogenic bacteria, leaving commensal microbes unaffected.   
2) Nanoparticles can disrupt the balance of the gut microbiome by killing beneficial microbes, potentially leading to dysbiosis.   
3) The gut microbiome has no influence on the stability or efficacy of nanoparticles in the gastrointestinal tract.

6) Advances in genomics have eliminated concerns about microbiome disruption by new therapies.   
7) Nanoparticles are unable to penetrate microbial biofilms in the gut environment.

Now we are able to identify where and how disturbances in the microbiota, or dysbiosis as it is referred to, may lead to the development of disease. This area of research is in urgent need of attention since natural selection against antibiotics is proving to be too great a hurdle to overcome. It is crucial to identify novel dysbiostatic drugs that will help, on one hand, to prevent dysbiosis and, on the other hand, to reduce the incidents of natural selection that lead to the development of antibiotic resistance in pathogenic bacteria [6]. Although the interactions between nanoparticles that reach the gastrointestinal tract and microbiota are far from being understood, there is now clear experimental evidence that nanoparticles may have debilitating effects against human microbiota. question:
Microbiome research investigates how the diversity and composition of microbial communities influence health and disease, especially in response to perturbations like antibiotics. Models and metrics are used to characterize these complex ecosystems and guide clinical and experimental decisions.

Which statement best explains why using phylogenetic diversity as a sole metric may be insufficient for assessing microbiome health following antibiotic treatment?

1) Phylogenetic diversity only measures the number of taxa present and ignores their evolutionary relationships.   
2) Phylogenetic diversity cannot account for changes in antibiotic resistance genes within the microbiome.   
3) Phylogenetic diversity may overlook functional redundancy, where distinct taxa perform similar ecological roles, leading to similar ecosystem function despite taxonomic differences.   
4) Phylogenetic diversity is superior to ecological distance in all controlled system analyses.   
5) Phylogenetic diversity consistently correlates with disease risk across all body sites and microbial habitats.   
6) Phylogenetic diversity is unaffected by sample size and thus always provides precise estimates.   
7) Phylogenetic diversity directly measures metabolic pathway abundance in the community.
answer: The correct answer is 3) Phylogenetic diversity may overlook functional redundancy, where distinct taxa perform similar ecological roles, leading to similar ecosystem function despite taxonomic differences..

question:
Probiotics are increasingly utilized in swine production to reduce reliance on antibiotics and enhance animal health and productivity. Lactic acid bacteria (LAB) are among the most studied probiotic organisms for their multifaceted benefits in pig diets.

Which of the following is NOT a demonstrated mechanism by which lactic acid bacteria (LAB) improve the gut health of pigs?

1) Stimulating the production of immunoglobulins and cytokines   
2) Strengthening intestinal tight junctions to maintain barrier function   
3) Producing organic acids, hydrogen peroxide, and bacteriocins to inhibit pathogens   
4) Competing with pathogens for intestinal adhesion sites and nutrients   
5) Enhancing the microbial balance within the gastrointestinal tract   
6) Directly promoting the genetic modification of pig intestinal cells   
7) Reducing the incidence of diarrhea and improving growth performance
answer: The correct answer is 6) Directly promoting the genetic modification of pig intestinal cells.
text: Title: The Use of Lactic Acid Bacteria as a Probiotic in Swine Diets Year: 2015 Paper ID: 119855040880e2783a27076eb25f440ea294dec1 Abstract: As the resistance of pathogens to antibiotics and the possibility of antibiotic residues in animal products attract increasing attention, the interest in the use of alternatives to in-feed antibiotics has been growing. Recent research with Lactic acid bacteria (LAB) in pigs suggests that LAB provide a potential alternative to antibiotic strategies. LAB include Lactobacillus species, Bifidobacterium spp, Bacillus spp, and some other microbes. LAB can adjust the intestinal environment, inhibit or kill pathogens in the gastrointestinal tract and improve the microbial balance in the intestine, as well as regulate intestinal mucosal immunity and maintain intestinal barrier function, thereby benefiting the health of pigs. The related mechanisms for these effects of LAB may include producing microbicidal substances with effects against gastrointestinal pathogens and other harmful microbes, competing with pathogens for binding sites on the intestinal epithelial cell surface and mucin as well as stimulating the immune system. In this review, the characteristics of LAB and their probiotic effects in newborn piglets, weaned piglets, growing pigs and sows are documented.

3) Fur metalloregulator
